chef_bio.chef_name: 原田浩司（株式会社GRACE 代表取締役）
chef_bio.origin: 京都市南区（創業地、2021年末まで）→ 2022年に伏見区へ移転
chef_bio.background: 鴨LABO grew out of a duck wholesaler's move into ramen — a shop opened beside the company's processing operation in Minami Ward, then relocated at the turn of 2021-2022 to its current home on National Route 1 in Fushimi, beside Jōnangū Shrine, for easier access and a roomier space. The name reads as a 'laboratory' for exploring what duck meat can be.
chef_bio.philosophy: Operating as a duck wholesaler's own restaurant, the shop treats itself as a 'lab' for the possibilities of duck — sourcing its own birds and serving everything from ramen to roast duck, minced duck, and takeaway duck hot-pot/shabu sets, so guests can enjoy duck casually day-to-day or as a small occasion.
chef_bio.specialty: Ramen built on domestic crossbred duck (aigamo / 国産あい鴨): the broth carries the deep umami and natural sweetness of duck yet stays light and refined rather than heavy. It runs across shio, shoyu, miso, and a signature kamo tantan-men with minced duck; the duck salt ramen (鴨塩ラーメン) is the reviewer favorite. Rice bowls include duck-loin, duck-chashu and minced-duck (soboro) don.

anecdotes.text: The shop is the ramen arm of a duck wholesaler that 'knows duck inside out,' giving it direct access to domestic aigamo duck and letting it sell duck chashu, minced duck, and duck hot-pot/shabu sets to take home alongside the bowls.
Reviewers describe the duck salt ramen as a mellow, refreshing bowl with a 'healing' (癒し) quality, served in a relaxed, spacious roadside space just south of Jōnangū Shrine's west torii on Route 1.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Ramen noodles are wheat-based (one account notes whole-wheat / 全粒粉 flour), so the bowls are not gluten-free and there is no indication of separate gluten-free preparation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Shoyu and tantan/miso bowls plus duck teriyaki rice bowls and gyoza rely on standard (wheat-based) soy sauce and seasonings; no wheat-free tare is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are duck-based and the menu is centered on duck meat throughout, so there is no plant-based broth to protect from cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, roadside ramen shop with parking and no English-specific service noted — a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will carry you through comfortably.

kyr_daikoku_ramen_honten.gf_detail: No gluten-free provision. This is a classic pork-bone-and-chicken shoyu ramen shop: the bowls use wheat (medium-thin) noodles and a soy-sauce-based tare that in this style is virtually always wheat-containing, and the popular yakimeshi (fried rice) is also seasoned with soy sauce. There is no published allergen information and no celiac-safe option. Not suitable for someone who must avoid gluten.
kyr_daikoku_ramen_honten.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The single signature ramen is a pork-bone and chicken-bone broth, topped with char siu (pork), and the house yakimeshi contains char siu and egg. There are no vegetable or vegan ramen options. A vegan would not have a meal here.
kyr_daikoku_ramen_honten.notes: [Mom & Pop] A neighborhood ramen institution that opened in 1983 and has anchored the old Nara highway in Fushimi for roughly four decades. The shop occupies a renovated former sake brewery (旧酒蔵を改装), fitting for the famous sake district, and is marked by a tricolor red-yellow-navy awning. It

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood ramen institution that opened in 1983 and has anchored the old Nara highway in Fushimi for roughly four decades. The shop occupies a renovated former sake brewery (旧酒蔵を改装), fitting for the famous sake district, and is marked by a tricolor red-yellow-navy awning. It is the original 本店 (main store) of a small local chain.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep it simple and generous: serve one well-made bowl at an affordable price so customers leave full, and welcome them back with a 100-yen discount voucher. As the shop puts it, they want people to eat their fill of good ramen at a reasonable price.
chef_bio.specialty: A single, focused bowl of tonkotsu-shoyu (豚骨醤油) ramen: a golden broth simmered from pork and chicken bones, kept clean and light-bodied (サラッとした味わい) rather than heavy, paired with medium-thin noodles. The other star is the yakimeshi (fried rice) of diced char siu, egg and green onion fried to a fluffy, separated texture; locals famously order ramen and yakimeshi together.

anecdotes.text: Founded in 1983 with a four-decade single focus on tonkotsu-shoyu ramen, the shop hands every departing customer a 100-yen discount voucher to encourage their return.
The yakimeshi is so beloved that nearly every customer orders it alongside their ramen; the shop operates out of a renovated former sake brewery on the old Nara highway.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and bowls use a soy-sauce-based tare; no gluten-free handling is offered.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone soy sauce) base; the shoyu tare in this style is virtually always wheat-containing.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is simmered from pork and chicken bones and bowls are topped with char siu pork; there are no vegan items and no separate preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, no-frills local ramen counter with no English support or allergen info, so a guide is recommended for diners with strict dietary needs.

kyr_ramen_monsen_fushimi_sak.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles (sourced from the Kyoto maker Menya Teigaku) and the chicken broth is almost certainly seasoned with wheat-based shoyu tare; the signature sake-lees (kasu) topping is fermented from rice but the noodles and seasoning are wheat. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no allergen handling is mentioned by any source. A celiac diner should treat this as unsafe.
kyr_ramen_monsen_fushimi_sak.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The house broth is a rich chicken-bone (tori-paitan / tori-gara) stock simmered with vegetables, and bowls are topped with chicken and other animal items. The sake-lees variations are also built on the same chicken base. No vegan or vegetarian ramen option is advertised.
kyr_ramen_monsen_fushimi_sak.hours_raw: 11:00-22:00 (L.O. 21:30); closed Tuesdays (open if Tuesday is a public holiday).
kyr_ramen_monsen_fushimi_sak.notes: [Mom & Pop] Monsen is a Kyoto chicken-broth ramen house whose flagship is in Gion, with branches in Kiyamachi and here in Fushimi. The Fushimi Sakagura-ten sits inside Fushimi Sakagura Koji, a nostalgic food-court alley of around nine eateries in Fushimi-Momoyama, one of Japan's three great

chef_bio.origin: Fushimi, Kyoto (within the Fushimi Sakagura Koji complex)
chef_bio.background: Monsen is a Kyoto chicken-broth ramen house whose flagship is in Gion, with branches in Kiyamachi and here in Fushimi. The Fushimi Sakagura-ten sits inside Fushimi Sakagura Koji, a nostalgic food-court alley of around nine eateries in Fushimi-Momoyama, one of Japan's great sake-brewing districts, where you can cross-order dishes between shops over a glass of local sake.
chef_bio.philosophy: A bowl that could only exist in Fushimi: letting guests taste the character of the surrounding sake breweries through the lees that finish a carefully simmered chicken broth.
chef_bio.specialty: Their signature is the 'kuramoto-ga-eraberu sakekasu ramen' (brewery-selectable sake-lees ramen), a bowl exclusive to this Fushimi branch. A long-simmered chicken-bone-and-vegetable tori-paitan broth is finished with sake lees that lends a rich, remarkably smooth body and a gentle sake aroma; diners pick their lees from a rotating lineup of local Fushimi breweries (about eight on offer, such as Kizakura, Tsukinokatsura, Hoshuku, Tamanohikari, Eikun, Kyohime, Miyakotsuru and Tomio). Thin, curly noodles from the established Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teigaku cling to the broth.

anecdotes.text: Letting customers choose their sake lees from the rotating lineup of nearby breweries is described as a service unique to Fushimi, where so many brewers are clustered together.

This branch carries Fushimi-only items not found at other Monsen shops, including the 'Montetsu ramen' (門鉄らーめん) done in collaboration with the neighboring teppanyaki spot 伏水 焼鉄 and a lighter 'sake-tori ramen' balancing chicken and sake-lees flavor.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No source documents the tare composition, but a chicken-broth ramen of this style is conventionally seasoned with wheat-based shoyu; not confirmed gluten-free.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: LOUD, and the same shape as the いしる case in the brief: we pinned this shop's gluten on an assumed soy tare while its real, documented gluten sat unnamed on the very page we cited. The page names Menya Teigaku wheat noodles, a カレーラーメン, and a lunch set of 唐揚げ + 餃子 + カレー — Japanese curry roux is wheat-

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is a chicken-bone (tori-gara/tori-paitan) stock simmered with vegetables, so no bowl is free of animal product even before toppings.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual counter-and-table ramen spot inside a lively Fushimi food-court alley; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will carry you, though dedicated English support is not advertised.

kyr_ra_mendokoro_katsukyo.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop: house-blended wheat noodles (fine to thick), miso and shoyu tare, and broths built on pork bone, chicken, and dried-fish/seafood stocks. Miso and soy-based tare typically contain wheat. No gluten-free menu, no gluten-free noodle option, and no allergen labeling is published. A celiac diner cannot eat safely here.
kyr_ra_mendokoro_katsukyo.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. Every broth is animal-based — domestic pork bone, free-range chicken, and seafood/dried-fish stocks — and signature bowls feature seared chashu pork, fish, and tuna rice sides. No plant-based broth or vegan ramen is offered.
kyr_ra_mendokoro_katsukyo.hours_raw: Mon, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sun: 11:00-14:00 and 17:30-21:00 (L.O. 20:30); Tue: 11:00-14:00 only; Sat: closed.
kyr_ra_mendokoro_katsukyo.notes: Katsukyo began in Shizuoka in October 2006, opened a second shop in Machida, Tokyo in June 2017, and brought the operation to its current spot in Fukakusa — on Shidan-dori between Fushimi Inari and Ryukoku University — in October 2019. It sits in a student-heavy neighborhood and

chef_bio.origin: Shizuoka, then Machida (Tokyo), now Fukakusa, Kyoto
chef_bio.background: Katsukyo began in Shizuoka in October 2006, opened a second shop in Machida, Tokyo in June 2017, and brought the operation to its current spot in Fukakusa — on Shidan-dori between Fushimi Inari and Ryukoku University — in October 2019. It sits in a student-heavy neighborhood and has built a steady local following.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's stated creed is that 'dashi is Japanese culture' (出汁は日本の文化). Broths are built entirely by hand — pork bone, chicken, and dried-fish/seafood stocks each simmered and refined over one to two days, strained meticulously and rested in cold storage to mature, with no chemical seasonings or instant products (無化調), aiming for a lower-sodium, body-friendly bowl. Ingredients are chosen with care: wild southern (minami) tuna sourced from Yaizu in Shizuoka, naturally sun-dried nori, domestic pork and free-range chicken, house-made menma, and a custom noodle blend rested three days.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a rich, deep miso ramen (the 特製味噌 / special miso) layered with pork-bone, seafood and vegetable umami, served over house-made thick, flat wavy noodles and topped with seared chashu, two kinds of green onion, mizuna and nori. The lineup also runs to a seafood-tonkotsu, a shoyu-tonkotsu line and tsukemen, with rice sides such as a seared-mackerel and a wild tuna (toro maguro) bowl.

anecdotes.text: The owner carried the shop across the country — founding it in Shizuoka in 2006, moving to Machida in Tokyo, then resettling in Fukakusa, Kyoto in late 2019 — before landing in this student quarter near Ryukoku University.
Its wild southern tuna is brought in directly from Yaizu in Shizuoka, a nod to the shop's Shizuoka roots, and appears on the menu as a toro-maguro rice bowl alongside the ramen.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water; the kitchen handles wheat noodles, miso/soy tare and flour-thickened broths throughout, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Shoyu-tonkotsu bowls and the miso tare rely on standard Japanese soy/miso seasoning, which typically contains wheat; no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are animal-based (pork bone, chicken, seafood/dried fish) and there is no separate plant-based stock, so no dish can be made vegan.

positives.text: Broths are made entirely from scratch with no chemical seasonings or instant products, simmered and matured over one to two days, with a stated low-sodium, body-friendly aim.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, cash-only counter ramen shop with a ticket vending machine and no English menu published — basic Japanese or pointing at the ticket machine makes the visit smooth.

kyr_ramenya_tamin.gf_detail: No gluten-free provision. This is a standard ramen shop: wheat ramen noodles in a rich chicken/pork-bone broth. There is no published indication of gluten-free noodles or any allergen accommodation, and the shop is a one-person operation with a single counter, so cross-contact is unavoidable. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_ramenya_tamin.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The broth is animal-based (chicken / chicken-pork bone, with one source noting a sea-bream-and-chicken base) and bowls are topped with pork chashu and menma. No plant-based or vegetable ramen is offered. Vegans cannot eat here.
kyr_ramenya_tamin.hours_raw: Business days and hours are irregular and announced on the owner's Twitter as they go. As a rough past guide: lunch ~12:00-14:00, dinner ~18:00-21:00 (varies with sourcing and prep). Checking social media before visiting is essential.
kyr_ramenya_tamin.notes: [Mom & Pop] らーめんや たみん is a one-person neighborhood ramen counter tucked beside Ryukoku University Mae-Fukakusa Station in the Fukakusa area of Fushimi, occupying a spot once home to a shop called 金太 (Kinta). It is the kind of tiny, owner-run place that locals seek out rather than stumble upo

chef_bio.origin: 京都市伏見区深草（旧「金太」の場所）
chef_bio.background: らーめんや たみん is a one-person neighborhood ramen counter tucked beside Ryukoku University Mae-Fukakusa Station in the Fukakusa area of Fushimi, occupying a spot once home to a shop called 金太 (Kinta). It is the kind of tiny, owner-run place that locals seek out rather than stumble upon.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop runs on the owner's own rhythm: just five counter seats, a food-ticket system, and operating days announced as the prep allows on Twitter rather than a fixed calendar. Quality and freshness drive the schedule, and the owner personally warns each guest that the bowl arrives extremely hot.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a 濃厚ラーメン (rich, concentrated ramen) built on a thick, glossy chicken-and-pork-bone (鶏豚骨) broth, topped with notably generous, tender chashu sliced over a centimeter thick, scallion, and seasoned menma. Reviewers describe the soup as deeply umami yet gently salted rather than heavy-handed.

anecdotes.text: One regular food blogger wrote that it took roughly a year of attempts before he finally managed to get in, because the shop opens only on irregular days posted to Twitter.
On serving the rich bowl the owner cautions diners 「熱いので気を付けて下さい」 (please be careful, it's hot) — the concentrated broth comes out scalding.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single small counter run by one person serving wheat-noodle ramen; no separate preparation area, so gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are built on animal broth (chicken / chicken-pork bone) with pork chashu; no plant-based options, and everything shares the same pots.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny five-seat counter shop with irregular hours announced only on Twitter and a food-ticket system; comfortable for a confident solo or pair visit with some basic Japanese, less suited to groups or those needing English support.

kyr_raamen_miya.gf_detail: This is a traditional Kyoto-style shoyu-tonkotsu ramen shop. The noodles are wheat (medium-thick straight noodles supplied by Menya Tiekun), and the soy tare almost certainly contains wheat, served over a pork-bone broth. There is no gluten-free menu, no mention of allergen handling, and the kitchen is a single small operation with shared boiling water — not safe for celiac diners. No gluten-free options found in any source.
kyr_raamen_miya.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly shop. The entire concept centers on a pork-bone (豚骨) broth and an abundance of chashu (roasted pork belly) — the signature draw is a bowl piled with pork. No vegan or vegetarian ramen, and no plant-based options are mentioned in any source.
kyr_raamen_miya.hours_raw: Tue-Sun 07:00-14:00, closed Mon (closes once sold out)
kyr_raamen_miya.notes: [Mom & Pop] After more than ten years of training at Kyoto's legendary Honke Daiichi Asahi Honten near Kyoto Station, the owner struck out on his own and opened Raamen Miya in September 2023, on the former site of a beloved ramen shop (Banrai-ya) that had closed. It sits tucked beneath the M

chef_bio.background: After more than ten years of training at Kyoto's legendary Honke Daiichi Asahi Honten near Kyoto Station, the owner struck out on his own and opened Raamen Miya in September 2023, on the former site of a beloved ramen shop (Banrai / ばんらい) that had closed. It sits tucked beneath the Meishin Expressway overpass, between Keihan Fujinomori and the Takeda subway/Kintetsu station, slightly toward Takeda.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner deliberately lightened the broth compared to the richer Daiichi Asahi original so it would suit early-morning eating, leaning into the Kyoto tradition of 'asa-ra' (morning ramen). The menu is kept simple and honest: ramen, chashu, rice, and a chashu rice bowl.
chef_bio.specialty: An 'Akira-style' (Daiichi Asahi lineage) original Kyoto ramen: a clean pork-bone broth finished with a crisp, fragrant soy tare and crowned with sweet, fatty pork-belly chashu. The signature is the meat-heavy bowl (肉増し / chashu ramen) where slices of chashu are fanned across the surface like flower petals, mixing fatty and lean cuts — reviewers joke the chashu never seems to run out.

anecdotes.text: Despite opening at 7:00 a.m., the counter fills to capacity during breakfast hours — one writer arrived before 9 a.m. to find nearly every seat taken.
The shop opened in September 2023 on the former premises of the much-missed ramen shop Banrai (ばんらい).
The owner trained for over ten years at the famed Honke Daiichi Asahi Honten before opening his own shop.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the soy-based tare typically contains wheat, served over a pork-bone broth — not safe for gluten avoidance.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is finished with a soy (shoyu) tare in the Daiichi Asahi lineage; Japanese shoyu almost always contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is pork-bone (豚骨) based and bowls are topped with abundant pork chashu; no plant-based preparation exists.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locals-first morning ramen counter where ordering in basic Japanese is smoothest, though an English menu is available to help you point to what you want.

kyr_houmairou.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The shop's identity is its 自家製麺 (house-made wheat noodles), and the signature カラシソバ combines those wheat noodles with a mustard-vinegar-soy-sauce dressing (soy sauce normally contains wheat) over a chicken/kombu sauce. Dumpling wrappers (shumai, spring rolls) are also wheat. There is no gluten-free menu and wheat is central to nearly every dish.
kyr_houmairou.vegan_detail: No vegan options indicated. The kitchen is a Chinese eatery built around pork (酢豚), meat-filled spring rolls and shumai, and a chicken-and-kelp-based stock for the noodle dishes. The signature カラシソバ rests on a chicken/kombu sauce. No plant-based menu is advertised; a strict vegan would have nothing reliable to order here.
kyr_houmairou.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner, Tetsuo Aiba, entered an apprenticeship at age 16 at the celebrated Kyoto Chinese restaurant 鳳舞 (Houmai), where he handled the noodle-making. 鳳舞 — a landmark of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking — closed in 2009 (Heisei 21), and 鳳舞楼, opened in December 2015, carries on its li

chef_bio.background: The owner, Tetsuo Aiba, entered an apprenticeship at age 16 at the celebrated Kyoto Chinese restaurant 鳳舞 (Houmai), where he was in charge of the noodle-making. 鳳舞 — a landmark of Kyoto-style Chinese cooking — closed in 2009 (Heisei 21), and 鳳舞楼, opened in December 2015, carries on its lineage. Within that 鳳舞 family of successor shops, 鳳舞楼 is noted as the only one that makes its own noodles in-house.
chef_bio.philosophy: Aiba speaks of wanting to carry the flavor he inherited from his 鳳舞 master to people nationwide, not only in Kyoto, and refuses to compromise on the house-made noodles and the mustard seasoning.
chef_bio.specialty: カラシソバ (Karashi Soba) — the shop's number-one dish. House-made, very thin crinkled noodles — springy and made in-house, a rarity among 鳳舞's successor shops — are dressed with a mustard-vinegar-soy seasoning over a chicken-and-kombu-stock (鶏ガラ昆布) sauce loaded with vegetables; the sharp mustard kick is what makes it addictive.

anecdotes.text: The signature flavor was originally devised by Aiba's master at 鳳舞, the shop where he began training at sixteen; he has preserved it as a one-of-a-kind taste.
Even the shumai are wrapped in an ultra-thin house-made skin (自家製の超薄皮), reflecting the shop's commitment to making its noodles and wrappers from scratch.

In March 2024 the shop moved from its quieter Shinmachi-dōri spot to a far more accessible location right at the Karasuma-Imadegawa crossing, above the subway's Imadegawa station and diagonally across from Doshisha University.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature カラシソバ is dressed with a mustard-vinegar-soy-sauce blend; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the sauce as well as the noodles carry gluten.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, busy local Kyoto-Chinese counter eatery where ordering and dietary requests are easiest in Japanese; English support should not be assumed.

kyr_kanton_ryori_heian.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation. The signature karashi soba is made with wheat noodles, and Chinese-style dishes here use soy-sauce/seasoning bases that typically contain wheat. There is no indication of gluten-free menu items, separate preparation, or celiac-aware handling. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_kanton_ryori_heian.vegan_detail: Not a vegan/vegetarian establishment. The signature karashi soba contains shrimp, chicken, and a chicken-and-kombu broth, and the kitchen is built around meat and seafood Cantonese cooking. No documented plant-based ramen or vegan options. Vegans cannot be reliably accommodated.
kyr_kanton_ryori_heian.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Fri, Sat, Sun: 12:00-14:00 (lunch), 17:30-20:00 (dinner). Closed Wednesday and Thursday.
kyr_kanton_ryori_heian.notes: [Mom & Pop] A husband-and-wife team runs this tucked-away Cantonese kitchen in an old Gion building, carrying on the lineage of Hōbu (鳳舞), the legendary Kyoto Chinese restaurant often called the source of "Kyo-chuka" (Kyoto-style Chinese cooking).

chef_bio.background: A husband-and-wife team runs this tucked-away Cantonese kitchen in an old Gion building, carrying on the lineage of Hōbu (鳳舞), the legendary Kyoto Chinese restaurant often called the source of "Kyo-chuka" (Kyoto-style Chinese cooking).
chef_bio.philosophy: Quiet, homey hospitality over flash: a deliberately inconspicuous door, an intimate counter, and an owner who checks in on diners mid-meal so the place feels like eating at someone's home rather than a restaurant.
chef_bio.specialty: Karashi soba (カラシソバ) — wheat noodles tossed in mustard and topped with a savory sauce of shrimp, chicken, green onion, bamboo shoot, lettuce, and wood-ear mushroom, built on a chicken stock and Rishiri kombu base, offered in three spice levels playfully named like school grades (中学 middle-school / 高校 high-school / 大学 university).

anecdotes.text: The karashi soba descends from a famous dish at the now-closed Hōbu, a foundational name in Kyoto Chinese cuisine, so a bowl here is a taste of that vanished lineage.

The mustard is potent enough that even the medium level can make your nose tingle; diners pick their heat by 'school grade,' and the couple's own cartoon likenesses appear on the menu, said to resemble them closely.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The signature karashi soba uses wheat noodles and the kitchen is a small Cantonese operation cooking many wheat-containing dishes in shared woks, so cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Cantonese/Kyoto-Chinese seasonings and sauces here are based on standard soy sauce and Chinese condiments, which normally contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The signature dish and broth contain shrimp, chicken, and chicken-kombu stock; the kitchen centers on meat and seafood, so any dish risks animal-product cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, husband-and-wife hidden-gem in an old Gion mixed-use building with a warm, homey feel; little to no English, so basic Japanese or a translation aid and a relaxed attitude help a lot.

kyr_ramen_okura_ichijoji_ten.gf_detail: Standard Japanese ramen shop with no gluten-free offering. Bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles, the shoyu/shio tare is almost certainly wheat-based soy sauce, and broths are pork/seafood based — not celiac-safe. There is no published allergen menu, dedicated prep, or GF noodle option. A celiac diner cannot eat safely here.
kyr_ramen_okura_ichijoji_ten.vegan_detail: Not a vegan/vegetarian-friendly shop. The broths are animal-based (pork/chicken and a seafood-blend "shin-gyokai" stock made from ten kinds of fish), toppings center on chashu pork, and sides include karaage and gyoza. No plant-based ramen is offered.
kyr_ramen_okura_ichijoji_ten.hours_raw: 11:00-05:00 (next day) daily; lunch sets available 11:00-14:00. (Note: the English Tabelog listing shows an older 11:00-22:00 with Tuesday closed; HotPepper/Gnavi list 11:00-05:00 open year-round.)
kyr_ramen_okura_ichijoji_ten.notes: [Mom & Pop] Ramen Okura sits on Ichijoji's famous ramen street in northeast Kyoto, a short walk from Eizan Ichijoji Station. It's a small, no-frills counter shop marked by a large red lantern and a neon sign, the kind of place that runs from lunch deep into the early morning for students, ni

chef_bio.background: Ramen Okura sits on Ichijoji's famous ramen street in northeast Kyoto, a short walk from Eizan Ichijoji Station. It's a small, no-frills counter shop, the kind of place that runs from lunch deep into the early morning (to 5 a.m.) for students, night workers and ramen-crawlers.
chef_bio.philosophy: Generous portions and honest value: lunch sets (until 14:00) add just 50 yen to a bowl and come with free rice refills, and the U-shaped counter is built so a solo diner can slip in and eat well without ceremony.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen lets you pick your broth: shoyu, shio, a punchy garlic bowl, a rich kotteri, and a 'new seafood' (shin-gyokai) ramen built on a stock blended from ten kinds of fish for a clean, collagen-rich umami. The back-fat shoyu is a Kyoto-standard animal-based bowl; the garlic ramen is a local favorite.

anecdotes.text: The 'new seafood' ramen leans on a broth made from ten types of fish ground to a powder and simmered in, giving a fish-forward, collagen-rich bowl the shop markets as especially popular with women (女性におすすめ).
Beyond ramen the menu spreads into pork rice bowls, karaage, gyoza and kimchi — set up as a late-night neighborhood spot rather than a single-bowl specialist.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Shoyu and shio tare at a standard Japanese ramen shop are made with conventional wheat-based soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is indicated.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: This is the soy-sauce-from-genre defect, and it is aimed at the wrong bowl. The shoyu half is fine to keep as an explicit inference (a しょうゆラーメン is on the menu, and no gluten-free soy sauce is indicated anywhere — that part is true). But 'shio tare ... made with conventional wheat-based soy sauce' is

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are animal-based (pork/chicken and a ten-fish seafood blend) and the shared kitchen also fries karaage and cooks gyoza, so no plant-based bowl can be assumed clean.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 9-seat late-night counter on Ichijoji's ramen street with no English support or allergen handling — comfortable to visit with a guide who can navigate the cash-only ordering and language.

kyr_ramen_nagata.gf_detail: Standard wheat ramen: straight wheat noodles in a chicken broth seasoned with a shoyu (wheat-containing soy sauce) tare, plus an abura soba (wheat noodle) option. No gluten-free items or accommodations are indicated. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_ramen_nagata.vegan_detail: Every bowl is built on chicken broth (the shop uses female local chicken bones), with pork chashu, and the broth/tare contain animal products throughout. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.
kyr_ramen_nagata.hours_raw: Tue-Sat 11:00-14:00 (L.O. ~14:30 per Tabelog) and 17:00-21:00; Sun & holidays 11:00-15:00; closed Monday. Sources vary slightly on lunch close (14:00 on blogs, 15:00 on Tabelog) and evening open (17:00 vs 17:30).
kyr_ramen_nagata.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner took up ramen seriously later in life, studying the craft on his own after turning 50, and opened this small shop in a quiet Kitashirakawa residential corner just south of the famous Ichijoji ramen district on October 14, 2021. Despite the weathered, old-fashioned lante

chef_bio.background: The owner took up ramen seriously later in life, studying the craft on his own after turning 50, and opened this small shop in a quiet Kitashirakawa residential corner (near Chayama Station on the Eizan line, just south of the famous Ichijoji ramen district) on October 14, 2021. Despite the weathered, old-fashioned lantern signage that makes it look like a decades-old institution, it is a relatively new arrival.
chef_bio.philosophy: He set out simply to become the neighborhood's beloved ramen shop, building bowls on pure chicken stock with female local chicken and refusing to muddy the soup. Offering a plain kake ramen for just 500 yen is read as quiet confidence in the broth and noodles alone.
chef_bio.specialty: Chicken-forward ramen made entirely from poultry stock. The clear shoyu chuka-soba is the chef's calling card, with a clean, transparent broth and medium-straight noodles, while the rich tori-paitan (chicken white broth) is praised as so deep it tastes almost like it contains pork bones. The Half & Half pairs a transparent shoyu seitan broth beneath the creamy chicken paitan in a single bowl that grows richer as you stir.

anecdotes.text: The chef began studying ramen independently after turning 50 and opened the shop on October 14, 2021, driven by the wish to become a local favorite.

The signature shoyu broth is made from female chicken bones and described as a clear, nostalgic Showa-era soup with a sharp soy finish, served with tender grilled chashu; an oversized soy-and-garlic karaage is a beloved side.
The Half & Half layers a clean shoyu seitan broth beneath a rich chicken paitan, so the bowl transitions from light to increasingly rich as the diner mixes it.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shoyu (soy sauce) tare that flavors the broth is standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run neighborhood counter shop with no English menu noted; basic Japanese or a translation app will help.

kyr_kyoto_ramen_kinzan_shich.gf_detail: Not suitable for celiac/strict gluten-free diners. The ramen is wheat noodles (from Kondo Seimen) in a pork-bone broth seasoned with wheat-based aged soy sauce tare. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated preparation, and shared wheat-noodle boiling water create unavoidable gluten exposure. No published allergen accommodation.
kyr_kyoto_ramen_kinzan_shich.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly option. The house specialty is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth finished with back fat and topped with two kinds of pork chashu; even the soy tare sits on an animal base. No plant-based broth or vegan bowl is offered.
kyr_kyoto_ramen_kinzan_shich.hours_raw: 11:30-14:30 / 18:00-23:30 (last orders 14:30 and 23:30). Closed Sundays plus occasional irregular closures. Note: an English listing alternatively shows 11:30-14:00 / 18:00-02:00 daily, so confirm before a late visit.
kyr_kyoto_ramen_kinzan_shich.notes: [Mom & Pop] Kinzan opened in 2013 in the quiet Nishioji-Shichijo residential pocket of Shimogyo-ku, a roughly 15-minute walk from JR Nishioji Station. The owner trained at the respected Takabashi Ramen before striking out on his own, and the shop has since grown into a local favorite popular

chef_bio.background: Kinzan opened in 2013 in the quiet Nishioji-Shichijo residential pocket of Shimogyo-ku, a roughly 15-minute walk from JR Nishioji Station. The owner trained at the respected Takabashi Ramen before striking out on his own, and the shop has since grown into a local favorite popular enough to open a second branch near Kyoto City Hall (Shiyakusho-mae).
chef_bio.philosophy: A Kyoto-rooted approach: classic local-style tonkotsu-shoyu done with carefully chosen regional ingredients (Kyotanba/Kyoto Highland pork from Hiyoshi Farm, Kujo negi, aged soy from the Koyama and Goko breweries, Kondo noodles), cooked in an open kitchen so guests can watch the bowl come together.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a 'Kyoto black shoyu' (京都黒醤油) ramen: a glossy, near-jet-black soup built on a pork-bone base, given sharpness and depth by aged soy sauce and a mellow sweetness by back fat. It is finished with two styles of Kyoto Highland pork chashu (lean and fatty, torched to order), Kujo green onion, bean sprouts, menma, and a slick of back fat. Straight medium-thin noodles from the long-established Kondo Seimen give a firm, wheaty bite.

anecdotes.text: The owner trained at the well-regarded Takabashi Ramen before opening Kinzan in 2013.
The chashu is cut from Kyoto Highland (Kyotanba) pork raised at Hiyoshi Farm and torched to order, and the noodles come from the long-established Kondo Seimen.
Students get a discount (about 100 yen off, with a free size-up).

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi confirms the 2013 founding, an ex-Takabashi Ramen owner, the 京都黒醤油 signature, Kyoto Highland pork from Hiyoshi Farm, Kujo negi, Kondo Seimen noodles and Koyama/Goko soy; a directly-run second shop (市役所前店) opened near City Hall in autumn 2023.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water, and the soy-sauce tare is wheat-based, so gluten contact is inherent to every bowl.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The black soup is seasoned with aged soy sauce (from Oyama and Goko breweries), which is wheat-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone based and finished with back fat; pork chashu tops the bowls, so there is no vegan-safe preparation line.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, busy neighborhood ramen counter with ticket-style ordering and an open kitchen; little to no English, so a few basic Japanese phrases (or pointing at the menu) make it smoother.

kyr_701_taresoba_kyoto.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. The dish is wheat ramen noodles dressed with a soy-sauce-based tare (soy sauce contains wheat), white vinegar and chili oil, topped with pork chashu. No GF noodles, GF tamari, or allergen accommodation is advertised anywhere. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_701_taresoba_kyoto.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian options. Every taresoba bowl comes with pork-belly chashu, and toppings/sides lean on meat (assorted chashu, mini chashu rice bowl) and egg (onsen tamago). The tare is soy-sauce based with no advertised plant-only build. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_701_taresoba_kyoto.notes: [Mom & Pop] Osamu Shinkai, a Tokyo native, spent years as a head chef in hotel Chinese and yakiniku kitchens before relocating to Kyoto in 2023 to open his own counter shop devoted to a single idea.

chef_bio.background: Osamu Shinkai, a Tokyo native, spent years as a head chef in hotel Chinese and yakiniku kitchens before relocating to Kyoto in 2023 to open his own counter shop devoted to a single idea.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than building a bowl around a rich broth, the shop strips the soup away entirely so the noodles themselves take center stage, with a sauce blended in a 'golden ratio' meant to flatter the noodle and let diners boldly mix and customize to taste.
chef_bio.specialty: Taresoba (soupless mixed noodles): the signature soy-sauce bowl tops springy noodles with pork-belly chashu, chopped onion, white sesame, scallion and bamboo shoot, which you mix vigorously with a tare of special soy sauce, oil, white vinegar and umami chili oil before eating; spicy and chilled mustard-sauce versions round out the lineup.

anecdotes.text: The shop opened on September 22, 2023 on a quiet lane near Hankyu Karasuma in central Kyoto's Nakagyo-ku, bringing a Tokyo-born take on soupless ramen to the city center.
Diners are encouraged to fine-tune noodle firmness and topping amounts, and to add the table-side white vinegar and rayu themselves before mixing.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tare is built on a special soy sauce, which in Japan is standard wheat-brewed shoyu; combined with wheat noodles this bowl is not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every bowl is finished with pork-belly chashu and shares a counter kitchen with meat and egg toppings, so no plant-only preparation is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 11-seat counter shop where ordering is simple (pick a sauce, mix it yourself) and a few words of Japanese plus pointing will carry you through comfortably.

kyr_mazemen_puruda.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle mazesoba shop. The signature bowl is built on wheat ramen-style noodles tossed with a savory tare, topped with chashu (pork), soft egg, menma, Korean seaweed and scallion. Wheat noodles plus a typically wheat-based shoyu-style tare and pork toppings make this unsuitable for celiac diners. No gluten-free preparation, no dedicated equipment, and no allergen handling is advertised. Not safe for gluten-free.
kyr_mazemen_puruda.vegan_detail: The only documented bowl is animal-based: chashu pork, soft-boiled egg, menma and Korean seaweed over wheat noodles, with no advertised vegetarian or vegan option. There is no indication any plant-based version is available. Not suitable for vegans.
kyr_mazemen_puruda.hours_raw: 11:00-14:00 (lunch only); the same premises operates as a Korean restaurant in the evening. Irregular closures.
kyr_mazemen_puruda.notes: [Mom & Pop] A daytime-only mixed-noodle counter near Kyoto Station's Hachijo exit that shares its kitchen with a Korean restaurant. By day the six seats are devoted to mazesoba; by night the same room becomes the Korean spot Hanbaibo Puruda (韓杯房プルダ). The mazesoba operation opened on July 3,

chef_bio.background: A daytime-only mixed-noodle counter near Kyoto Station's Hachijo exit that shares its kitchen with a Korean restaurant. By day the six seats are devoted to mazesoba; by night the same room becomes the Korean spot Hanbaibo Puruda (韓杯房プルダ). The mazesoba operation opened on July 3, 2025.
chef_bio.specialty: Mazesoba (mixed noodles), regular size around 1,000 yen, topped with chashu pork, soft-boiled egg, menma, Korean seaweed and shredded scallion, with an optional soft-cooked egg add-on. The Korean-seaweed topping nods to the kitchen's evening Korean identity.

anecdotes.text: The mazesoba shop opened July 3, 2025, occupying the lunch hours of a space that serves as the Korean restaurant Hanbaibo Puruda in the evenings.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 6-seat counter lunch spot with no English advertised; a little Japanese and pointing at the single mazesoba goes a long way.

kyr_kyoto_toripaitan_soba_ju.gf_detail: This is a chicken-paitan ramen specialist built around custom medium-thick wheat noodles served in a creamy chicken-and-pork-bone broth, with seasoning tare and shoyu/miso variants that typically contain wheat. No gluten-free noodle, dedicated prep, or celiac accommodation is mentioned anywhere. Not safe for celiacs; a strictly gluten-free diner should not eat here.
kyr_kyoto_toripaitan_soba_ju.vegan_detail: Every bowl is built on an animal base: a rich chicken (tori-paitan) broth made primarily with Kagoshima chicken, supplemented with Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and topped with rare pork chashu. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options listed. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_kyoto_toripaitan_soba_ju.hours_raw: Lunch 11:00-15:00 (L.O. 14:30); Dinner 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:30). Closed Wednesdays per local guides; the official site states year-round open with no Obon closure, so hours may vary — confirm before visiting.
kyr_kyoto_toripaitan_soba_ju.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner Sakakimoto came to ramen the long way around, spending some fifteen years training in kappo (Japanese fine-dining) and sushi kitchens before striking out on his own. That fine-dining grounding shows in every detail of the bowl.

chef_bio.origin: This is the second outpost of the Jun chicken-paitan brand, following the original near Marutamachi; it opened in the Shijo-Karasuma area on August 13, 2025.
chef_bio.background: Owner Sakakimoto came to ramen the long way around, spending some fifteen years training in kappo (Japanese fine-dining) and sushi kitchens before striking out on his own. That fine-dining grounding shows in every detail of the bowl.
chef_bio.philosophy: Sakakimoto has said that if he was going to open his own place, he wanted to do something only he could do — hence the labor-intensive, single-serving emulsified broth and the kappo-trained attention to finish and presentation.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a tori-paitan (chicken white-soup) soba in an espuma-like, foamed broth. Rather than ladling from one big pot, the kitchen emulsifies the chicken soup bowl by bowl in a blender, whipping it into a mild, airy, almost cappuccino-like froth. The base is built primarily on Kagoshima chicken, rounded out with small amounts of Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and paired with custom medium-thick, chewy noodles and rare pork chashu.

anecdotes.text: The bowl is built to be played with: a trio of flavored vinegars (including apple and orange) let you tune the soup as you go, and regulars finish by adding rice to the leftover broth for a carbonara-like second act.
Unlike the original Marutamachi shop, this branch adds wontons and rare chashu to the lineup, with a yuzu-salt foamed chicken paitan and a miso version among the headline bowls.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shoyu and miso seasoning variants of the chicken-paitan soba are based on tare/sauces that conventionally contain wheat; no wheat-free seasoning is indicated.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: There is no shoyu bowl at this branch, so the record warns about a seasoning the shop does not sell, and the one tare the operator documents is 塩ダレ. Replace the claim with the wheat that is actually on the menu and far more certain: ワンタン wrappers are the default upsell on all three bowls, the noodle

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are animal-based (chicken paitan plus pork bones) and bowls are topped with pork chashu, so there is no vegan-safe preparation; cross-contact with meat and animal stock is inherent.

cultural_comfort.note: A modern, tidy counter shop comfortable for newcomers and overseas visitors, though staff likely operate mainly in Japanese, so a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu go a long way.

kyr_toyojiro.gf_detail: This is conventional Jiro-style ramen: wheat noodles plus a soy-sauce (shoyu) or salt tare, served in an animal-fat broth. Wheat noodles and standard shoyu both contain gluten, and no gluten-free option or gluten-handling practice is mentioned anywhere. Not suitable for celiacs; treat as unsafe.
kyr_toyojiro.vegan_detail: A Jiro-style ramen shop built around a beef-fat broth (rendered fat from 48-month-old female cattle), wheat noodles, and beef-tendon (bokkake) toppings. There is no vegan or vegetarian bowl here; the entire concept is meat-forward, so a plant-based diner has nothing safe to order.
kyr_toyojiro.hours_raw: 11:00-22:00, open daily (no regular closed day listed). Note: the ramen offering reportedly runs alongside the evening izakaya operation; lunchtime is recommended for the ramen without a mandatory drink order.
kyr_toyojiro.notes: [Mom & Pop] Toyojiro opened on December 1, 2024 in the Kawaramachi area of Kyoto, growing out of the popular Kiyamachi tuna-and-wagyu izakaya Toyota and sharing its premises. It represents that team's leap from sake-side beef and tuna plates into a dedicated Jiro-style ramen concept.

chef_bio.background: Toyojiro opened on December 1, 2024 in the Kawaramachi/Kiyamachi area of Kyoto (Yaoyacho, Nakagyo-ku), growing out of the popular tuna-and-wagyu izakaya Toyota (とよ田) and sharing its premises. It represents that team's leap from sake-side beef and tuna plates into a dedicated Jiro-style ramen concept.
chef_bio.philosophy: To elevate the famously rough, fat-heavy Jiro genre with high-grade wagyu fat rather than ordinary pork back-fat, aiming for a smooth, deep umami that gives ramen fans a more refined take on the style.
chef_bio.specialty: A wagyu-forward Jiro-style bowl: a broth built on rendered fat from 48-month-old female cattle from Okazaki Ranch, finished with a soy-sauce or salt tare and crowned with premium wagyu fat. The house signature carries over the izakaya's bokkake (slow-stewed beef tendon) as a topping, giving a bokkake-jiro that fuses wagyu and ramen.

anecdotes.text: The shop is an offshoot of the tuna-and-wagyu izakaya Toyota and runs from the same Yaoyacho premises, carrying over that bar's signature bokkake (stewed beef tendon) into the ramen.
The broth's defining ingredient is fat from 48-month-old female cattle from Okazaki Ranch, chosen for its melt-on-the-tongue quality and deep umami.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are offered in a soy-sauce (shoyu) or salt tare; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and no wheat-free tare is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is made from rendered beef fat and the toppings are beef tendon and wagyu fat, so the entire kitchen workflow is meat-based.

cultural_comfort.note: A small counter ramen shop sharing premises with an izakaya; no English information is available, so a visitor will likely need a guide or translation help to navigate ordering and the Jiro-style customs.

kyr_menya_ichiki.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature bowl is built on wheat ramen noodles and is topped with fresh fu (生麩, wheat gluten), so there are multiple unavoidable wheat sources in the dish itself. The broth is a white-miso tare with bonito/kombu dashi (miso typically contains wheat or barley as well). No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or celiac accommodation is indicated. A celiac diner cannot eat the ramen here safely.
kyr_menya_ichiki.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. Both signature bowls are built on animal stock — bonito (katsuobushi)/kombu dashi or a shellfish (kai) dashi — and are topped with smoked chashu pork and a soft-boiled egg. While the yuba (tofu skin) and fresh fu toppings are plant-based, the broth foundation is fish/shellfish-based, so the ramen is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. No vegan version is advertised.
kyr_menya_ichiki.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 / 17:00-20:30 (may close once soup runs out). Closed days irregular - specific weekday closures not published, so the same hours are listed for all days with an irregular-schedule flag.
kyr_menya_ichiki.notes: [Mom & Pop] Menya Ichiki bills itself as a Kyoto white-miso ramen specialist. It first opened on October 6, 2025 as a tucked-away shop in the Nishijin area of Kamigyo Ward, then relocated and reopened on April 22, 2026 in a renovated Kyoto townhouse (machiya) in Shikino Higashino-cho, in the

chef_bio.background: Menya Ichiki bills itself as a Kyoto white-miso ramen specialist. It first opened on October 6, 2025 as a tucked-away shop in the Nishijin area, then relocated and reopened on April 22, 2026 in a renovated Kyoto townhouse (machiya) in Shikino Higashino-cho, Kita Ward, along Kitaoji-dori near Kenkun Shrine and Daitoku-ji.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop leans into local Kyoto identity — white miso, yuba and fu — to set its bowls apart from typical tonkotsu or shoyu ramen, and keeps a calm, welcoming room where even solo diners are at ease.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the 京の白味噌らーめん (Kyo no Shiro-miso Ramen): an original tare blending several Kyoto white misos for a gently sweet, creamy soup, married to a bonito-and-kombu dashi. A variation, the 京の白味噌貝だしらーめん, swaps in a shellfish (scallop) dashi for a mellower umami. Bowls come dressed in distinctly Kyoto ingredients — fresh yuba (tofu skin) and fresh fu (wheat gluten) — alongside smoked chashu pork, a soft-boiled egg, white negi and bonito flakes. The chashu is torched just before serving to coax out its aroma and umami. Thick, straight noodles with a firm chew round it out. A rice-and-fried-chicken set can be added.

anecdotes.text: Promoted as one of Kyoto's first white-miso ramen specialty shops, leaning on Kyoto white miso, fresh yuba and fresh fu for a distinctly local bowl.
Opened October 6, 2025 as a hidden-gem shop in a Nishijin residential neighborhood, then relocated and reopened April 22, 2026 in a renovated machiya near Kenkun Shrine.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The dish itself contains multiple wheat sources — wheat ramen noodles plus a fresh fu (wheat gluten) topping — so cross-contamination is moot; the ramen is inherently not gluten-free.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a white-miso tare; Kyoto white miso commonly contains wheat or barley, and the dashi is bonito/kombu or shellfish based. No wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is built on bonito/kombu or shellfish dashi and bowls include smoked chashu pork and egg; plant toppings (yuba, fu) sit in an animal-based soup, so a vegan-safe bowl is not offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood ramen specialist in a renovated machiya; menus and service are in Japanese, so a translation app or some basic Japanese helps, though ordering a signature bowl is straightforward.

kyr_menya_kagari_kiyamachi_t.gf_detail: A standard ramen shop: wheat noodles with a chicken/seafood (and tonkotsu) broth and a soy-based tare, which means wheat is present in both the noodles and the seasoning. No gluten-free menu, gluten-free noodles, or allergy accommodation is mentioned anywhere. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_menya_kagari_kiyamachi_t.vegan_detail: All bowls are built on animal broths (chicken paitan, seafood, tonkotsu) and topped with seared chashu pork, so nothing on the menu is vegan. The fresh yuba (tofu skin) topping that is the shop's signature is itself plant-based, but it is served in meat/fish broth, so it does not make any bowl vegan. No vegan option is offered.
kyr_menya_kagari_kiyamachi_t.hours_raw: 21:00-06:00 (through to the next morning). One source lists daily operation; another notes closed Wednesdays.
kyr_menya_kagari_kiyamachi_t.notes: [Mom & Pop] Menya Kagari's Kiyamachi branch is a small, hard-to-find ramen shop tucked into a back alley off Kiyamachi Street, just a few minutes from Kyoto Kawaramachi Station. It keeps unusual late-night-into-dawn hours (roughly 9 p.m. to 6 a.m.), which has made it a quiet institution for

chef_bio.background: Menya Kagari's Kiyamachi branch is a small, hard-to-find ramen shop tucked into a back alley off Kiyamachi Street, just a few minutes from Kyoto Kawaramachi Station. It keeps unusual late-night-into-dawn hours (roughly 9 p.m. to 6 a.m.), which has made it a quiet institution for night-shift workers winding down, drinkers looking for a closing bowl, and early risers wanting ramen for breakfast.
chef_bio.philosophy: A neighborhood late-night refuge built around comforting, broth-forward bowls and a hidden-gem atmosphere rather than flash.
chef_bio.specialty: The kitchen offers a rich, opaque chicken paitan alongside a cleaner chicken-and-seafood soy broth and a heavier tonkotsu. Its most distinctive bowl is a Kyoto-style ramen finished with fresh yuba (tofu skin): the delicate sheets soak up the soup and add a soft, local character you rarely see on a ramen counter. A charred-garlic black ramen rounds out the late-night lineup.

anecdotes.text: Regulars describe it as a hidden gem worth the hunt down a Kiyamachi side alley near H&M, prized for its fresh-yuba ramen that pairs surprisingly well with the soy broth.
Locals favor it as a late-night and post-drinking spot as well as an early-morning meal, thanks to its 21:00–06:00 hours.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop's soy-based (shoyu) ramen uses a standard soy tare, which in Japanese ramen virtually always contains wheat; combined with wheat noodles this bowl is not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bowls are built on chicken, seafood, and tonkotsu (pork) broths and topped with seared chashu pork; the plant-based yuba topping is served in these animal broths.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, locals-oriented late-night counter shop with no listed English support, so basic Japanese and a willingness to point at the menu will make ordering easiest.

kyr_kumamoto_ramen_higo_mokk.gf_detail: This is a classic Kumamoto-style tonkotsu ramen shop. The noodles are wheat, and the tare/seasoning and accompaniments (gyoza, karaage, paiku rice simmered in soy sauce) are wheat-based. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is advertised; not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_kumamoto_ramen_higo_mokk.vegan_detail: The entire menu is built on a rich pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth with pork toppings, plus chicken karaage and soy-braised pork rice. No vegetarian or vegan ramen is offered.
kyr_kumamoto_ramen_higo_mokk.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small ramen counter sitting steps from Kitayama Station and across from the Kyoto Prefectural Botanical Garden, serving the Kumamoto style of tonkotsu in a city better known for lighter Kyoto ramen. The name itself is a wink to its roots: 'mokkosu' is Kumamoto dialect for a stu

chef_bio.background: A small ramen counter sitting steps from Kitayama Station and across from the Kyoto Prefectural Botanical Garden, serving the Kumamoto style of tonkotsu in a city better known for lighter Kyoto ramen. The name itself is a wink to its roots: 'mokkosu' is Kumamoto dialect for a stubborn, headstrong, true-to-yourself sort of person.
chef_bio.philosophy: Diners describe an owner with a meticulous, conscientious touch in the service and presentation, leaning into a robust, full-bodied bowl rather than the lighter Hakata-style tonkotsu.
chef_bio.specialty: Kumamoto ramen: a thick, milky-white tonkotsu (pork-bone) broth finished with fragrant burnt-garlic ma-yu oil, served with thin, straight noodles. A favorite side is the paiku rice (パイクごはん): pork rib cartilage braised sweet-and-spicy until meltingly tender, collagen-rich and juicy, served over rice.

anecdotes.text: The shop name 'mokkosu' comes from Kumamoto dialect meaning a stubborn, headstrong person, signaling its proudly Kumamoto identity in Kyoto.
Its tonkotsu is noted as concentrated and rich yet surprisingly clean-tasting, finished with burnt-garlic ma-yu oil that tames any pork-bone odor.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyoto-gourmet and Tabelog confirm a Kumamoto tonkotsu shop by Kitayama Station opposite the Botanical Garden, with 焦がしニンニク油 (ma-yu), thin straight noodles, and パイクごはん = braised pork rib cartilage over rice.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water; not gluten-free.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Paiku rice is pork simmered in a soy-based sauce, and tonkotsu tare typically uses wheat-containing soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone based with pork and chicken items throughout the menu; no vegan-safe preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood ramen counter; expect Japanese-only ordering, so a little Japanese or pointing at the menu helps.

kyr_no_ko_tonkotsu_ramen_iwa.gf_detail: This is a Yokohama iekei (家系) ramen shop built on wheat ramen noodles (from Tokyo's Sugano Seimen / 菅野製麺所), a wheat-based shoyu tare, and a thick pork-and-chicken bone broth — none of which is gluten-free. No gluten-free noodles, tare, or menu options are advertised, and there is no indication of allergen handling. Not suitable for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.
kyr_no_ko_tonkotsu_ramen_iwa.vegan_detail: A pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken broth iekei specialist; the signature bowl is topped with chashu pork, spinach, and nori. The broth, tare, and toppings are animal-based with no vegan or vegetarian ramen offered. Not suitable for vegans.
kyr_no_ko_tonkotsu_ramen_iwa.hours_raw: 11:00-1:00 the next day (L.O. 0:30, closes once soup runs out), open daily
kyr_no_ko_tonkotsu_ramen_iwa.notes: [Mom & Pop] Iwamotoya occupies the former 麺匠 一粒万倍 西院店, a branch of a Kyoto ramen group known for lighter chicken-based clear shoyu bowls. chef_bio.background: Iwamotoya occupies the former 麺匠 一粒万倍 西院店, a branch of a Kyoto ramen group known for lighter chicken-based (Oyama jidori and duck) clear shoyu bowls. That Saiin location — the one shop in the group that had long served iekei — closed on August 3, 2025 and reopened on August 11, 2025 as a dedicated Yokohama-style iekei (家系) tonkotsu-shoyu shop aimed at late-night and younger diners in the Saiin area.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than leaning on surface oil, the shop builds its identity on a genuinely concentrated, dense broth that still keeps a proper drinkable fluidity — an honest take on iekei conventions that aims for real depth of bone-and-marrow character rather than formulaic repetition.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a straightforward iekei 'Ramen' (around 950 yen): a thick pork-and-chicken bone broth with a soy tare, topped in classic family-style fashion with a slice of chashu pork, spinach, and three sheets of nori. The noodles are sourced from Tokyo's well-known Sugano Seimen (菅野製麺所) and served a touch shorter than typical iekei noodles, with a rice pairing available.

anecdotes.text: The shop is a full rebrand of the former 麺匠 一粒万倍 西院店, swapping that group's signature light chicken-shoyu style for a bold tonkotsu iekei concept when it reopened on August 11, 2025.
A ramen critic praised the broth as '濃厚で濃密な味わい' (concentrated, dense), noting the shop achieves legitimate originality within iekei conventions while staying authentically in the category.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core menu is wheat ramen noodles in a shared pot, with a wheat-based shoyu tare and animal broth; no gluten-free preparation or separation is described.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: An iekei tonkotsu-shoyu shop whose tare is soy-sauce based; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, and no wheat-free tare is offered.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone and chicken based and bowls are topped with chashu pork; no vegan or vegetarian option exists, so meat-free dining is not viable.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No allergen information or accommodation is noted in available reviews or shop information.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, cash-only late-night ramen counter where ordering is quick and simple; a guide or basic Japanese helps, as English support and allergen accommodation should not be assumed.

kyr_raizanken.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation. This is a classic Kyoto-style chuka soba shop: wheat ramen noodles in a chicken-and-pork shoyu broth, where the soy-based tare almost certainly contains wheat. Sides (gyoza, fried chicken, egg-rice sets) are also wheat/flour-based. Not suitable for celiacs; no dedicated handling found.
kyr_raizanken.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly shop. The signature bowls are built on a chicken-bone and pork-bone broth with a touch of back-fat, and the menu centers on chashu ramen, gyoza, and meat/egg sets. No plant-based ramen or vegan options were found.
kyr_raizanken.hours_raw: Mon-Fri and holidays (excluding Sun) 11:30-14:30, 17:30-23:30 / Sat and holidays 11:30-14:30, 17:30-23:00
kyr_raizanken.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-standing neighborhood machi-chuka (town Chinese) diner sitting almost on top of Goryo Station on the Kyoto subway Tozai line, the kind of homey, street-side counter spot where local families and solo regulars have eaten for years.

chef_bio.background: A homey neighborhood noodle-shop (shokudo) standing right in front of Goryo Station on the Kyoto subway Tozai line in Yamashina Ward — the kind of street-side counter spot, with 16 seats (an 8-seat counter and two four-tops), where local families and solo regulars have eaten for years.
chef_bio.philosophy: Approachable, homemade comfort food at honest prices, welcoming to solo diners, families, and groups alike.
chef_bio.specialty: Budget neighborhood noodle-shop fare: a light shoyu ramen alongside a wafu (Japanese-style) ramen and a curry ramen, plus gyoza and affordable rice-and-set combinations, with most bowls coming in under about 1,000 yen.

anecdotes.text: The shop sits directly in front of Goryo Station in Yamashina and serves classic, budget-friendly noodle-shop fare — shoyu and wafu ramen, curry ramen, gyoza and rice sets — in a 16-seat room.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog and Gnavi list Raizanken as a ramen/udon diner (食堂) directly in front of Goryo Station in Yamashina, 16 seats, serving shoyu/wafu/curry ramen, gyoza and rice sets under ~1,000 yen; it is not documented specifically as a Chinese (machi-chuka) specialist.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the broth/tare is built on a wheat-containing soy base; no gluten-free preparation exists here.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Shoyu-forward Kyoto-style tare; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and there is no indication of a wheat-free alternative.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is chicken- and pork-bone based with back-fat; menu is meat- and egg-centric, so cross-contact with animal products is pervasive throughout the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly, no-frills neighborhood diner run for locals; expect Japanese-only service and a casual, all-smoking room, so a little Japanese and easygoing manners go a long way.

kyr_aburasoba_daikakumei_kin.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle abura soba / ae-men shop. The noodles are wheat, the tare (sauce that coats the bowl) is soy-sauce-based and almost certainly contains wheat, and toppings include pork. There is no indication of any gluten-free option, gluten-free noodle, or allergy accommodation. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoidant diners.
kyr_aburasoba_daikakumei_kin.vegan_detail: The core dish is built on pork (chashu / pork belly, meat-topped bowls) and a soy-based tare; meat-miso and meat-topped bowls are the signatures. There is no vegan or vegetarian bowl on the menu and no plant-based broth option. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kyr_aburasoba_daikakumei_kin.notes: [Mom & Pop] A short walk from the famous Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji), this is a casual, student-favorite noodle counter that started life in August 2021 as a branch of the abura-soba franchise Kirin-ji (きりん寺). In April 2025 the shop broke from the franchise and went independent under the bo

chef_bio.background: A short walk from the famous Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji), this is a casual, student-favorite noodle counter that started life in August 2021 as a branch of the abura-soba franchise Kirin-ji (きりん寺). In late April 2025 the shop broke from the franchise and went independent under the bold new name 大革命 ("Great Revolution"). True to the name, the owner kept tinkering: around August 2025 the menu shifted away from classic oil-based abura soba toward oil-free あえ麺 (ae-men), where the sauce is mixed through the noodles rather than pooling with oil at the bottom of the bowl.
chef_bio.philosophy: Hearty, junky, build-your-own-flavor comfort food that proposes 'a new way to enjoy abura soba' — a deliberate contrast to Kyoto's refined kaiseki tradition, aimed at filling up students and travelers cheaply and boldly.
chef_bio.specialty: The shop made its name on the 肉盛り油そば (meat-piled abura soba) — chewy, slightly wavy wheat noodles under a generous heap of soft, tender pork, eaten by mixing in chili oil (rayu) and vinegar to taste, with grated garlic and spicy meat-miso on the table to fine-tune each bite. In the ae-men era this carries over into hearty bowls like a niku-miso (spicy meat-miso) ae-men, often paired with karaage and rice as a set.

anecdotes.text: The name 大革命 ('Great Revolution') marks the shop's independence from the Kirin-ji franchise in spring 2025, and the owner lived up to it by later dropping oil entirely and reworking the dish into mixed ae-men.

A Yahoo! News ramen expert highlighted the roughly ¥1,000 niku-mori abura soba as a 'junk and wild' Kyoto gem within walking distance of Kinkaku-ji, praising the tender, generous pork and chewy noodles.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dish is built on a soy-sauce-based tare mixed through wheat noodles; standard Japanese soy sauce tare contains wheat, making the sauce as well as the noodles unsuitable for gluten avoidance.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: No page anywhere names a soy tare for this shop. The record should either drop the soy-sauce assertion or rewrite it as an explicit cuisine-convention inference. Two further staleness problems on the same record: (a) the shop stopped selling 油そば in August 2025 and dropped the word from its name — it

vegan_cross_contact.text: Bowls center on pork (chashu / pork belly) and meat-miso, with karaage on set menus; the kitchen is meat-forward and offers no plant-based bowl.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, no-frills counter noodle shop popular with local Ritsumeikan students; staff are unlikely to speak much English, so order by pointing or a few Japanese words and you'll be fine.

kyr_kuso_oyaji_saigo_no_hito.gf_detail: Standard ramen: wheat (medium-thick straight) noodles plus a soy-sauce-based tare (typically wheat-containing). Not celiac-safe and no gluten-free menu is indicated. The broth itself is clam dashi, but the noodles and shoyu tare make the dish unsafe for gluten avoidance.
kyr_kuso_oyaji_saigo_no_hito.vegan_detail: This is a shellfish-broth ramen specialist — every bowl (asari/shijimi/hamaguri) is built on a clam dashi with soy-sauce tare and contains clams; there are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options.
kyr_kuso_oyaji_saigo_no_hito.hours_raw: 11:00–23:00 daily (last order around 22:30–23:30 depending on source; press release states 11:00–24:00 L.O. 23:30; Tabelog lists 11:00–23:00)
kyr_kuso_oyaji_saigo_no_hito.notes: This is the first Kyoto location of くそオヤジ最後のひとふり, a clam-broth ramen brand under Osaka's UNCHI Co., the company behind the celebrated 'Jinrui Mina Menrui' (人類みな麺類). The original Kuso Oyaji opened in Osaka's Juso district in April 2013, and the brand has since reached overseas mar

chef_bio.background: This is the first Kyoto location of くそオヤジ最後のひとふり, a clam-broth ramen brand under Osaka's UNCHI Co., the company behind the celebrated 'Jinrui Mina Menrui' (人類みな麺類). The original Kuso Oyaji opened in Osaka's Juso district in April 2013, and the brand has since reached overseas markets including New York, China, Korea and Nepal. The Kawaramachi-Sanjo shop opened September 15, 2023, set into the Sanjo shopping arcade with a refined Japanese-style interior — counter seats on the first floor and tables on the second (about 19 seats in all).
chef_bio.philosophy: The parent company's stated guiding idea is to 'change the world through the power of ramen,' and the broths are made with custom water-purification equipment to draw out a clean shellfish umami meant to be finished to the last drop.
chef_bio.specialty: Clam-broth ramen, with the あさりラーメン (asari/short-neck clam ramen, around 980–990 yen) as the signature bowl — a clean clam dashi balanced with a blend of dark and light soy sauce, served with chewy yet firm medium-thick straight noodles and clams as a topping. The shijimi (corbicula) and a limited hamaguri (clam) ramen round out the lineup.

anecdotes.text: The Osaka original opened in Juso in April 2013 and the brand has since expanded internationally to New York, China, Korea and Nepal before this first Kyoto outpost.
About a week after opening, an evening visit around 7 PM found roughly ten groups waiting in line — a sign of the strong early buzz around the Kyoto debut.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: PRTimes (UNCHI press release) confirms April 2013 Juso origin, 'change the world through ramen' mission, custom water-purification broth, three clam varieties, ¥980 asari ramen, overseas branches (NY/China/Korea/Nepal) and the Sept 15 2023 Kawaramachi-Sanjo opening. Tabelog confirms 19 seats split 1F counter (10) / 2F tables (9). A local blog notes ~10 groups queuing a week after opening.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowls are built on a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare — described as a blend of dark and light soy sauce over clam dashi — which typically contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All ramen is shellfish-based (clam dashi with clam toppings); there is no vegan/vegetarian preparation, so cross-contact with shellfish is inherent to the menu.

source_independence.note: This source reprints shop marketing rather than reporting a visit (a curated hub or a press release). It corroborates that a claim was MADE, not that it was verified.

cultural_comfort.note: A busy, popular ramen counter where you queue and order at the counter; little English support is expected, so a non-Japanese speaker may want a translated menu or guidance, but pointing at the clam-ramen options works fine.

kyr_yakimeshi_to_men_kyoto.gf_detail: No gluten-free option. The signature bowls are built on house-made wheat noodles (a Hokkaido "yume-chikara" wheat blend with whole-grain flour) in a pork-and-seafood shoyu broth, so the noodles, the soy-based tare, and the fried rice all contain wheat. There is no indication of any GF menu, dedicated equipment, or allergy accommodation. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner cannot eat safely here.
kyr_yakimeshi_to_men_kyoto.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The broth is a pork-and-dried-fish (niboshi/katsuobushi) double stock, the bowls feature rare char siu (pork), and the fried rice contains roast pork and egg. There are no plant-based ramen or rice options noted. A vegan would have nothing suitable to order.
kyr_yakimeshi_to_men_kyoto.hours_raw: Weekdays (Mon–Fri): 11:00–15:00 and 17:30–21:00. Saturdays, Sundays and holidays: 11:00–21:00 (continuous). Oil-based ramen (abura soba) served only from 15:00. Last order around 21:00.
kyr_yakimeshi_to_men_kyoto.notes: [Mom & Pop] Yakimeshi to Men Kyoto opened on April 2, 2025 in the Sanjo-meiten-gai arcade just west of Kawaramachi-Sanjo, as the second location of a brand built by the people behind the well-regarded Osaka-area ramen shop Chuka Soba Fumoto (中華そば ふもと) in Hirakata. The concept is right in the

roles: Operated by the team behind the Osaka-area shop 中華そば ふもと (Fumoto)
chef_bio.background: Yakimeshi to Men Kyoto opened on April 2, 2025 in the Sanjo-meiten-gai arcade just west of Kawaramachi-Sanjo, as a sister shop from the team behind the well-regarded Osaka-area ramen shop Chuka Soba Fumoto (中華そば 麓/ふもと). The concept is right in the name and refreshingly honest: 'we want to eat fried rice AND we want to eat noodles' — so rather than treating the rice as an afterthought side, the shop puts equal craft into both.
chef_bio.philosophy: Take both halves of the classic machi-chuka pairing seriously — neither the noodles nor the rice plays second fiddle. Yuzu powder from Kochi and a grape-sansho (Japanese pepper) oil from Wakayama are set out so diners can tune the bowl to taste, and an evening-only abura soba (oil noodles, from 15:00) gives a different way to enjoy the same house noodles.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the char siu ramen paired with a half portion of fried rice (chashu-men half-yakimeshi set). The bowl is a pork-and-dried-fish double-stock shoyu ramen — pork depth lifted by niboshi (dried sardine) and a finish of shaved bonito — served with house-made straight noodles blending Hokkaido 'yume-chikara' wheat with whole-grain flour, boiled firm. It is crowned with petal-thin rare char siu (pork shoulder loin marinated in a red-wine-and-soy tare). The fried rice is its own point of pride: shredded roast pork and fluffy egg cooked to be moist yet crumbly, with dedicated rice cooked to order per portion.

anecdotes.text: The shop's name literally translates to 'Fried Rice and Noodles,' born from the idea that you shouldn't have to choose between the two — so the half-fried-rice set was made the headline order.
It sits in the Sanjo-meiten-gai arcade and quickly became part of a wave of new ramen shops turning the Sanjo–Kawaramachi blocks into a ramen battleground.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyo-soku and Osumituki confirm the April 2, 2025 opening, that it is run by/sister to Osaka's Chuka Soba Fumoto (麓), the chashu-men half-yakimeshi set, the pork+niboshi+bonito double broth, and house-made Hokkaido 'yumechikara' whole-grain noodles. Kyotopi calls it a sister shop (姉妹店) to Fumoto/Menfu, not a numbered branch. Sources describe the petal-thin rare pork-shoulder char siu in a red-wine soy marinade and yuzu-powder/grape-sansho-oil condiments.

gf_cross_contamination.text: House-made wheat noodles and wheat-based shoyu tare are central to every bowl, and fried rice is cooked on the same line — heavy shared wheat presence throughout the kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen and the char siu is marinated in soy sauce; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, so the tare and marinade should be assumed to contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is a pork-and-dried-fish (niboshi, bonito) stock and dishes feature pork char siu and egg; no plant-based preparation is mentioned.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, busy arcade ramen shop with no English menu noted; a friendly greeting and pointing at the signature set will carry you through, but staff are unlikely to navigate detailed dietary requests in English.

kyr_menshin_yoshida.gf_detail: A tsukemen specialist whose entire identity is its house-made wheat noodles (stone-ground whole-grain flour from Nagano blended with refined wheat). The dipping broths are wheat-thickened/seasoned and rich in shrimp, chicken and fish. There is no gluten-free noodle or menu, no dedicated equipment, and noodles are boiled in shared water — not suitable for celiac diners.
kyr_menshin_yoshida.vegan_detail: Every bowl is animal-based: the signature dip is built on more than a kilogram of sweet-shrimp heads, and the standard option is a chicken-and-seafood (鶏魚介) broth. No vegan or vegetarian option is offered.
kyr_menshin_yoshida.notes: [Mom & Pop] 麺心よし田 is the shop Fushimi locals name first when the talk turns to tsukemen. Tucked just west of Fushimi-Momoyama / Momoyama-Goryomae stations, past the Otesuji shopping arcade, it has built a devoted following over years — regulars describe coming back dozens of times since thei

chef_bio.background: 麺心よし田 is the shop Fushimi locals name first when the talk turns to tsukemen. Tucked just west of Fushimi-Momoyama / Momoyama-Goryomae stations, past the Otesuji shopping arcade, it has built a devoted following over years — regulars describe coming back dozens of times since their student days for noodles that taste reliably the same.
chef_bio.philosophy: The heart of the shop is the house-made noodle — milled from Nagano stone-ground whole-grain flour blended with refined wheat, giving a soba-like fragrance. The kitchen deliberately leaves the cold-rinsed noodles slightly moist, believing that texture carries the wheat aroma best, and serves regular and large portions at the same price.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a rich shrimp tsukemen (海老味噌つけ麺): a dipping broth built from more than a kilogram of sweet-shrimp heads simmered with vegetables, yielding a deep, almost French-bisque-like richness that earns it the nickname of a 'French-inspired' tsukemen. The classic alternative is a chicken-and-seafood (鶏魚介) dip.

anecdotes.text: The shop hands diners a posted 'way of eating' (流儀): start with the noodles as-is, then layer in onion and citrus to shift the flavor in stages, and finish the leftover dip as a consommé-style soup.
The shrimp dip is built from over a kilogram of sweet-shrimp heads, lending the broth its distinctive concentrated, bisque-like body.
A longtime regular writes of having visited dozens of times since student days, praising the unwavering consistency of the bowl.
anecdotes.source: https://minaju.info/lunch/2-16-京都市伏見区-伏見桃山-麺心-よしだ-つけ麺/

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Totteoki Kyoto (official tourism site) confirms the Fushimi-Momoyama/Otesuji location, house noodles from Nagano stone-ground whole-grain flour, the rich shrimp tsukemen built from 1kg+ of sweet-shrimp heads (French-bisque-like), the chicken-seafood dip, the posted 流儀 eating method (noodles first, then onion/citrus, finish the dip as soup), and same-price regular/large portions. A local blog corroborates the devoted-regular following.
sources: https://minaju.info/lunch/2-16-京都市伏見区-伏見桃山-麺心-よしだ-つけ麺/

gf_cross_contamination.text: Noodles are wheat-based (whole-grain + refined wheat flour) and boiled in shared water; no gluten-free option exists.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths are animal-based (sweet-shrimp heads, chicken, seafood); shared cookware means no vegan-safe preparation.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, locals-beloved counter shop with no English menu noted; basic Japanese and a willingness to follow the posted eating-order instructions will make the visit smooth.

kyr_kirin_en.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation found. This is a Cantonese Chinese restaurant whose signature is a chili-laden tantanmen — wheat noodles in a sesame/chili broth, almost certainly built on a wheat-based shoyu/miso tare and a pork base. No allergen or gluten-free information is published on the official site, and nothing indicates celiac-safe handling. A celiac diner should treat this place as not safe.
kyr_kirin_en.vegan_detail: Not a vegan venue. A traditional Cantonese kitchen with a meat- and seafood-forward menu (the famous tantanmen and black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork are both meat dishes). No vegan ramen or vegan set is advertised, and tantanmen broth is typically pork/sesame based. A vegan would need to ask, with little likelihood of a fully plant-based bowl.
kyr_kirin_en.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30–14:00; Dinner 16:30–23:00 (last order 22:30). Closed Tuesdays. (Tabelog lists lunch as 11:00–14:00; the official site states 11:30–14:00 — the official 11:30 start is used here.)
kyr_kirin_en.notes: Kirin-en opened in 1967, when authentic Cantonese cooking was still a rarity in the then-farmland district of Muko.
