Founder Miyaji Tamotsu set out to let local residents enjoy genuine Guangdong cuisine casually, and the place has stayed family-run, with Miyaji Ryo now serving as

chef_bio.background: Kirin-en opened in 1967, when authentic Cantonese cooking was still a rarity in the then-farmland district of Muko. Founder Miyaji Tamotsu (宮路保) set out to let local residents enjoy genuine Guangdong cuisine casually, and the place has stayed family-run, with Miyaji Ryo (宮路亮) now serving as store manager.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house motto for its spicy dishes is 「辛くて旨い」— 'spicy but delicious' (うま辛) — chasing flavor and craft rather than heat for its own sake.
chef_bio.specialty: A fiery tantanmen built on four kinds of chili plus a house-made meat-miso for depth, which became the restaurant's calling card during Muko City's spicy-food (gekikara) town-revitalization push. In developing it the kitchen reached for the bhut jolokia ('jolokia') pepper — once billed as the world's hottest — and the bowl can be ordered across escalating heat levels (roughly 1 to 5), with the mild steps served without the jolokia powder and the hottest tiers dosed with it.

anecdotes.text: Founded in 1967 by Miyaji Tamotsu to bring real Cantonese cooking to a Muko neighborhood that was still mostly farmland.
The tantanmen earned the Gold Grand Prix at the very first KARA-1 spicy-food competition, the contest run by Muko City's gekikara shopping district.
A quieter favorite is the black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork (黒酢酢豚), whose depth beneath the tang makes it a regulars' pick.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kirinen.com and the Otokuni-Kyoto guide confirm the 1967 founding by Miyaji Tamotsu (宮路保) with son/manager Miyaji Ryo (宮路亮), authentic Cantonese cooking in then-farmland Muko, the KARA-1 Grand Prix gold-winning tantanmen (four kinds of chili + house meat-miso, bhut/jolokia pepper 'world's hottest at development', selectable 1-5 heat levels), the 「辛くて旨い」うま辛 ethos, and the black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-noodle tantanmen cooked in shared pots in a Chinese kitchen that also fries and wok-cooks; no gluten-free handling is described anywhere.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a Cantonese restaurant and a tantanmen specialist, dishes rely on standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce and likely wheat-based tare; no wheat-free soy is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Meat- and seafood-forward kitchen with a pork/sesame tantanmen base; no separated vegan prep is indicated.

cultural_comfort.note: A long-running neighborhood Chinese restaurant where Japanese is the working language; a little prepared Japanese or a translation app will smooth ordering, and staff are used to spice-seekers from across Japan.

kyr_ramen_tengu_nishijin.gf_detail: A wheat-noodle ramen shop. The signature bowl is thin wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth blended with Japanese dashi, almost certainly built on a wheat-based shoyu tare, with chashu and menma. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, a dedicated preparation area, or allergen handling, and broth/tare are shared. Not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_ramen_tengu_nishijin.vegan_detail: The base of every bowl is an animal broth (pork bone blended with Japanese dashi), and toppings center on braised pork chashu. No vegetable or vegan broth, no plant-based ramen, and no meatless menu is described. Not a vegan-friendly option.
kyr_ramen_tengu_nishijin.hours_raw: 11:30-22:00 (Tabelog) / some articles list 11:30-23:00. Closed Wednesday (some reports say irregular closures).
kyr_ramen_tengu_nishijin.notes: [Mom & Pop] A modest, locally beloved ramen shop in the Nishijin district of Kyoto's Kamigyo ward, set along Chieko-koin street near the old textile quarter. It is the second location of Ramen Tengu, whose main shop is in Uzumasa in western Kyoto, and it carries a nostalgic Showa-era chuka-s

chef_bio.background: A modest, locally beloved ramen shop in the Nishijin district of Kyoto's Kamigyo ward, set along Chiekoin-dori (知恵光院通) near the old textile quarter. It is the second location (2号店) of Ramen Tengu, whose main shop is in Uzumasa in western Kyoto, and it carries a nostalgic Showa-era chuka-soba feel with a hand-painted sign and a cozy room of wrap-around counter and a few low tatami seats.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep it simple and let the broth do the work - a clean, comforting Kyoto-style bowl that regulars return for rather than a flashy specialty shop.
chef_bio.specialty: The house bowl, Tengu Ramen, is built on a pork-bone broth blended with Japanese-style dashi: it looks rich and is dressed with back-fat, yet drinks surprisingly clean and stays balanced to the last sip. It comes over thin, springy noodles with menma, nori and a chashu so slow-braised it falls apart and melts on the tongue. A generous heap of fresh, crisp scallions is served on the side so you can pile them in to taste, with an extra-scallion (追いネギ) option for about 50 yen.

anecdotes.text: The chashu is so tender that visitors joke about how many hours it must be simmered - it crumbles apart when lifted with chopsticks and enriches the broth as it dissolves.
The scallions arrive on a separate dish so diners can add as many as they like; an extra-scallions option (追いネギ, ~50 yen) lets you load the bowl up further.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi confirms the Nishijin (Kamigyo) location, that this is the 2号店 with the honten in Uzumasa (Ukyo-ku), the original pork-bone + Japanese-dashi broth that drinks light despite the back-fat, thin broth-clinging noodles with menma and nori, melt-apart chashu, and green onions served separately with a 追いネギ ¥50 add-on.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the broth is a pork-bone/dashi base with a presumed wheat shoyu tare; no gluten-free handling is described.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is described as a shoyu-style (soy-sauce) ramen, which in a shop like this is virtually always a wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are based on animal broth (pork bone plus Japanese dashi) and topped with pork chashu; no vegan or vegetable broth is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, local Nishijin ramen counter where ordering in Japanese and paying cash will go most smoothly; no English service is indicated.

kyr_ramen_kyoto_tengu_tokiwa.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop: the noodles are thin low-alkaline wheat noodles (mirroring the Sugichiyo lineage), the tare is soy-sauce based (shoyu, which in Japan virtually always contains wheat), and gyoza/shumai/shoronpo sides are wheat-wrapped. The pork-bone/chicken broth itself plus heavy shared-pot/shared-fryer use means cross-contamination is unavoidable. No gluten-free menu or noodle substitute is offered.
kyr_ramen_kyoto_tengu_tokiwa.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian establishment. The signature bowl is built on a pork-bone (tonkotsu) and chicken-gara broth finished with back fat (背脂), topped with chashu pork. The broth and the standard bowls are animal-based, so there are no genuine vegan or vegetarian ramen options here. A plant-based diner would have no suitable main; ask staff before ordering, but expect no accommodation.
kyr_ramen_kyoto_tengu_tokiwa.hours_raw: Lunch and dinner 11:30-2:00 the next day (L.O. 1:40). No regular closing day.
kyr_ramen_kyoto_tengu_tokiwa.notes: [Mom & Pop] Opened in 2002 by a chef who had been the head cook (店主／元料理長) at Sugichiyo (杉千代), a legendary Uzumasa ramen shop that drew lines for its then-revolutionary bowls some two decades ago. When Sugichiyo's original shop was gone, Tengu became the refuge for its devoted fans, carrying

chef_bio.background: Opened in 2002 by a chef who had headed the kitchen (店長／元料理長) at Sugichiyo (杉千代), a legendary Uzumasa ramen shop that drew lines for its then-revolutionary bowls some two decades ago. When Sugichiyo's original shop was gone, Tengu became the refuge for its devoted fans — described as the sole shop carrying Sugichiyo's DNA forward — and it is the original 2002 shop of the Ramen Kyoto Tengu group.
chef_bio.philosophy: Carry the Sugichiyo lineage faithfully rather than chase trends: an honest, additive-conscious pork-bone shoyu bowl in a modest storefront, kept welcoming for families, children and women rather than dressed up as a destination shop.
chef_bio.specialty: Tengu Ramen (てんぐラーメン): a pork-bone and chicken-gara shoyu broth finished with back fat (背脂) that drinks lighter than it looks, paired with thin low-alkaline straight noodles in the Sugichiyo mold and chashu so tender it falls apart when lifted with chopsticks. A basket of chopped green onion is provided to season the bowl to taste, and rice is famously all-you-can-eat.

anecdotes.text: The owner had headed the kitchen at the legendary Sugichiyo and founded Tengu in 2002, becoming the home for orphaned Sugichiyo fans.
The thin low-alkaline straight noodles deliberately mirror Sugichiyo's, and diners are handed a basket of chopped green onion to customize the bowl; the chashu is so soft it crumbles when picked up.
Regulars describe it as carrying on the lineage of the now-gone famous Sugichiyo ramen shop in Uzumasa, with all-you-can-eat rice as a signature touch.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Genjitsutouhi and Retty reviews confirm the Tokiwa (Ukyo-ku) shop was founded in 2002 by a former Sugichiyo (杉千代) head from Uzumasa, that it carries Sugichiyo's 'DNA' as the shop fans turned to, its pork-bone+chicken shoyu broth with back fat, thin low-alkaline Sugichiyo-style noodles, melt-apart chashu, a basket of chopped green onion, and all-you-can-eat rice (ライス食べ放題).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles cooked in a shared boiling pot, plus wheat-wrapped gyoza/shumai/shoronpo on the same line, make gluten cross-contamination unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is a shoyu (soy-sauce) style ramen; Japanese soy sauce almost always contains wheat, so the tare is a wheat source.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone and chicken-gara based and finished with pork back fat; chashu pork tops the bowl, so no dish is free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, unpretentious neighborhood ramen shop with tatami seating and a family-friendly feel; no English is advertised, so a guide or a few Japanese phrases will make ordering smoother.

kyr_ramen_senmonten_daiki.gf_detail: This is a traditional Kyoto-style ramen shop. The bowl is built on wheat noodles in a pork-based clear broth seasoned with a light soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which is wheat-based. Both the noodles and the tare contain wheat/gluten, and there is no gluten-free menu, no separate preparation, and no indication of allergy accommodation. This is not safe for celiacs or those avoiding gluten.
kyr_ramen_senmonten_daiki.vegan_detail: Every bowl is built on a pork bone broth (made from Miyazaki-raised pork) and topped with fatty chashu pork, so the soup itself is animal-based. There are no vegan or vegetarian options on the menu.
kyr_ramen_senmonten_daiki.hours_raw: Tue-Fri 11:00-15:00 / Sat and Sun 11:00-15:00, 17:30-20:00 / closed Mon and the 3rd Sun
kyr_ramen_senmonten_daiki.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small ramen specialist tucked into the Umezu neighborhood of Kyoto's Ukyo ward, near the Hankyu Matsuo-taisha line on the Arashiyama side of the city. The shop has been quietly perfecting one thing for over four decades, opening around 1981-1982 and, in the owner's own words, b

chef_bio.background: A small ramen specialist tucked into the Umezu neighborhood of Kyoto's Ukyo ward, on the Arashiyama side of the city near the Hankyu Matsuo-taisha line. The shop has been quietly perfecting one thing for over four decades, opening around 1981 and, in the owner's own words, building it up steadily over roughly 45 years in a corner of Kyoto.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner's stated aim is simple and warm: once a customer comes in, to earn their return and become a shop they patronize for a lifetime - 'a lifelong asset.' Guests are invited to step in without hesitation and give the ramen a try.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a Kyoto-style shoyu ramen in the Daiichi-Asahi (第一旭) mold: a pork clear-broth (tonkotsu seitan) made from Miyazaki-raised pork, seasoned with a light soy-sauce tare. Unlike many Kyoto bowls it skips the heavy back-fat float yet still drinks rich, with a generous layer of oil on top - mild in flavor but satisfyingly hearty. It comes crowned with soft, fatty melt-in-the-mouth chashu, thin bean sprouts, and Kujo green onion over thin, low-hydration straight noodles.

anecdotes.text: The chashu is made from fatty pork sourced from Miyazaki and is so tender it falls apart and melts in the mouth - a detail regulars single out as the highlight of the bowl.
The owner describes the shop as something built up steadily over about 45 years in one corner of Kyoto, and warmly invites newcomers to come in without hesitation and taste it once.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Osumituki (Kyoto ramen guide) places Daiki in Umezu, Ukyo-ku, dates it to roughly 1981 (~36 years as of 2017, i.e. ~45 now), and describes a Daiichi-Asahi-style Kyoto shoyu on Miyazaki pork with an oil float (not heavy back-fat), fatty melt chashu, fine bean sprouts, Kujo negi and thin low-hydration straight noodles. The shop's own site voices the 'lifelong patronage' aim.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The ramen uses wheat noodles cooked in shared water and a wheat-based light soy-sauce tare; there is no gluten-free preparation or separate handling.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is seasoned with a light soy-sauce (薄口醤油) tare, which is wheat-based as standard Japanese soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is a pork bone stock and the bowl is topped with pork chashu, so all menu items are animal-based; no vegan options exist.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, cash-only, counter-only neighborhood shop with no English menu or service; some basic Japanese or pointing at the simple ramen-and-chashu menu will make ordering smooth.

kyr_ryumon_honten.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation indicated. The noodle dishes (scallion-oil chicken noodles, hot-and-sour noodles) use wheat noodles, and Chinese cooking here relies heavily on wheat-based soy sauce and shared frying/wok surfaces. There is no evidence of allergen handling or a dedicated setup, so this is not a safe choice for celiac diners.
kyr_ryumon_honten.vegan_detail: Not a vegan venue. This is a full Sichuan Chinese restaurant built around pork, chicken, seafood and egg dishes. A few vegetable-forward plates exist (e.g. spicy stir-fried eggplant, eight-treasure mixed vegetables, garlic eggplant), but these are typically cooked with meat-based stock, oils, soy/oyster-style seasonings and shared woks, so they are not reliably vegan. Plant-based diners would need to ask, and even then options are narrow.
kyr_ryumon_honten.hours_raw: Tabelog lists 17:00–23:00 daily; the official site and local press describe the main branch as open 17:00 until 05:00 the next morning, a well-known late-night spot. No regular closing day; open year-round (one source notes Sundays closed, but most sources indicate daily operation — confirm by phone).
kyr_ryumon_honten.notes: Ryumon is widely regarded as one of Kyoto's pioneers of authentic Sichuan cooking, with its original Higashiyama-Sanjo location anchoring a small family of branches across the city. The main shop is run with a genuinely Chinese kitchen and floor — Mandarin is spoken throughout, a

chef_bio.background: Ryumon is widely regarded as one of Kyoto's pioneers of authentic Sichuan cooking, with its original Higashiyama-Sanjo location anchoring a small family of about four branches across the city. The main shop is run with a genuinely Chinese kitchen and floor — Mandarin is spoken throughout, and the cooking balances heat with depth rather than chasing pure spice.
chef_bio.philosophy: Honest, homestyle Sichuan food cooked the way it is in China — real Sichuan chilies and peppercorns, big flavors, late into the night — served in an unpretentious neighborhood setting.
chef_bio.specialty: The scallion-oil chicken noodles (葱油鶏面, ¥650) are the house signature — an inexpensive bowl that regulars describe as authentic enough to bring a tear to your eye. Alongside them, the fiery Sichuan-peppercorn stir-fried eggplant (¥950) and a properly numbing mapo tofu are the dishes locals come back for.

anecdotes.text: The shop draws not only Kyoto locals but visitors from across Japan and even diners from China seeking a taste of home, a marker of how authentic the cooking is.
The dining room is so thoroughly Chinese in feel that one writer joked the inside is 'practically China,' with Mandarin flying between the staff and Sichuan aromatics filling the air.
Regulars single out the 650-yen scallion-oil chicken noodles as 'delicious enough to cry over' and praise it as the real, local flavor.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi and Sotokoto confirm Ryumon as a Kyoto pioneer of authentic Sichuan cooking at Higashiyama-Sanjo (open until ~5am) with roughly four branches, a Chinese kitchen speaking Mandarin, the ¥650 scallion-oil chicken noodles ('泣くほどおいしい'), the Sichuan-peppercorn stir-fried eggplant (¥950), spicy mapo tofu, and diners from across Japan and China. No source states a specific 'Chengdu' style, so that qualifier was removed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sichuan Chinese cooking of this style relies on wheat-based soy sauce and seasonings; no gluten-free soy alternative is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetable dishes are cooked in shared woks alongside pork, chicken and seafood and commonly use meat-based stock and animal-derived seasonings; no vegan-separation practice is indicated.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, authentic late-night Chinese spot where Mandarin flies between staff; a little Japanese (or pointing at the menu) goes a long way, and the lively, no-frills atmosphere is welcoming rather than precious.

kyr_rosen.gf_detail: No gluten-free provision found. The house specialty is tantan-men, which is wheat noodles in a sesame-rich, meat-based sauce, and the kitchen is a Sichuan/Chinese operation that relies on wheat-based soy sauce and fermented bean paste (doubanjiang). Mapo tofu, yakisoba, and other listed dishes are all gluten-bearing. No dedicated gluten-free menu, no allergen labeling, and no cross-contamination controls were documented anywhere. Treat as not celiac-safe.
kyr_rosen.vegan_detail: Not a vegan or vegetarian-oriented shop. The signature tantan-men contains pork mince and meat/sesame sauce, and the broader Sichuan menu (mapo tofu, Peking duck, daily lunch sets) is built around meat and animal stocks. No vegan or vegetarian options were identified on any page. A vegan diner could not be reliably accommodated here.
kyr_rosen.hours_raw: 11:30-14:30 (L.O. 14:00) / 17:30-21:30 (L.O. 21:00); closed Wednesdays. (Some listings show 11:00-14:30 / 17:00-21:30; Tabelog gives the 11:30/17:30 times.)
kyr_rosen.notes: [Mom & Pop] Rosen is a small, calm one-story house restaurant in the Kashihara neighborhood of Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, a short ride from Hankyu Katsura Station. The proprietor trained at well-regarded Sichuan kitchens in the Kansai region and continues to travel to China, bringing that ground

chef_bio.background: Rosen is a small, calm house restaurant in the Kashihara neighborhood of Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, a short walk from Hankyu Katsura Station. Owner-chef Fukaya (深谷信人), a Kameoka native, trained from his teens — culinary school, then the celebrated Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) that once sat in Kyoto's Holiday Inn, followed by kitchens in Osaka and Nishinomiya — before going solo to Shanghai to study authentic Chinese cooking. He named the shop after Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan and opened in Kashihara about a dozen years ago, and he still hand-makes his doubanjiang, tianmianjiang and douchi and cooks with Kashihara- and Kameoka-grown vegetables.
chef_bio.philosophy: Authentic Sichuan and Chinese cooking served generously and affordably in an unfussy, settled space — confident portions and honest pricing rather than show, built on house-made seasonings and local produce.
chef_bio.specialty: Tantan-men is the house signature, offered in white-sesame and black-sesame versions (with a curry tantan-men alongside). The black-sesame bowl is the standout: a rich, deeply aromatic sesame sauce with gentle sweetness and restrained heat over springy noodles — mellow rather than fiercely spicy. The Sichuan mapo tofu comes in mild and tongue-numbing spicy versions, and a salt yakisoba on wide flat noodles finished with a touch of oyster sauce is a quieter favorite.

anecdotes.text: Owner-chef Fukaya, from Kameoka, worked his way through the famed Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) and kitchens in Osaka and Nishinomiya, then trained solo in Shanghai, naming the shop for Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan.
Lunch sets stay under about 900 yen and the dining room fills at midday, drawn by the fragrant tantan-men and the mapo tofu offered in both mild and tongue-numbing spicy versions.

A reviewer singled out the black-sesame tantan-men for its mellow, sweet-leaning sesame richness and good noodle bounce, and praised the salt yakisoba made with wide flat noodles finished with a touch of oyster sauce.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hankei Kyoto Shimbun profiles owner-chef 深谷信人 (Fukaya, 42, from Kameoka): culinary school from his teens, the Sichuan restaurant Kato Hanten (華都飯店) in the former Kyoto Holiday Inn, then Osaka and Nishinomiya, then solo study in Shanghai; the shop is named for Luzhou (瀘州) in Sichuan, opened ~12 years ago in Kashihara, hand-makes doubanjiang/tianmianjiang/douchi and uses Kashihara/Kameoka vegetables. Kyotopi and Gourpass confirm the white/black-sesame and curry tantan-men (mellow black-sesame standout), mild/spicy Sichuan mapo, salt yakisoba with oyster-sauce finish, and sub-¥900 lunches.

gf_cross_contamination.text: House specialty is wheat-noodle tantan-men prepared in a shared Sichuan/Chinese kitchen alongside other wheat-containing dishes (yakisoba, etc.); no gluten-free handling was documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sichuan and Chinese cooking here relies on standard wheat-based soy sauce and fermented bean paste; no wheat-free seasoning alternatives were mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Tantan-men contains pork mince and the menu centers on meat and animal stocks; no vegan/vegetarian preparation or separation was noted.

cultural_comfort.note: A neighborhood Chinese restaurant with no indication of English support, so arriving with your order chosen and a few Japanese phrases ready will make things smoothest.

kyr_tonkotsu_raamen_yoshihar.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. This is a classic wheat-noodle ramen shop — straight thin wheat noodles in a pork-bone broth, with gyoza (wheat skins) and fried rice/karaage on the menu. The tare and accompaniments almost certainly include wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated prep, or allergen accommodation is advertised on any source. A celiac diner should not eat the ramen here.
kyr_tonkotsu_raamen_yoshihar.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The entire identity of the shop is a pork-bone (plus chicken carcass and chicken-feet) broth simmered 24+ hours, topped with chashu pork. There are no vegetable- or vegan-broth options noted anywhere. Side dishes are rice/gyoza/karaage, also non-vegan. Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.
kyr_tonkotsu_raamen_yoshihar.hours_raw: Lunch: Tue-Fri 11:00-14:30, Sat-Sun/holidays 11:00-14:45. Dinner: Tue-Sat 17:30-22:00, Sun/holidays 17:30-21:30. Closed Mondays (or the following Tuesday when Monday is a holiday). Note: some listings show slightly different hours (e.g., dinner to 23:30 on Tabelog); the official site hours are used here.
kyr_tonkotsu_raamen_yoshihar.notes: [Mom & Pop] Owner-chef Shoichi Iwasaki spent roughly 15 years training at a celebrated tonkotsu ramen shop in Minoh, Osaka, before opening Yoshiharu in 2013. After leaving the kitchen where he learned his craft, he spent extensive trial-and-error developing the broth that would become the sh

chef_bio.origin: Opened March 2013 in the Nishinokyō neighborhood of Kyoto's Nakagyō Ward, near Nijō Castle and the Sanjō-kai shopping arcade.
chef_bio.background: Owner-chef Shoichi Iwasaki (岩﨑昭一) spent roughly 15 years training at a celebrated tonkotsu ramen shop in Minoh, Osaka — also his hometown — before opening Yoshiharu on March 11, 2013. After leaving the kitchen where he learned his craft, he spent extensive trial-and-error developing the broth that would become the shop's signature.
chef_bio.philosophy: Iwasaki aims for a broth that suppresses the heavy off-odor often associated with pork bone, delivering deep umami and richness with a clean, light finish — a balance of 'umami, richness, and depth.' The shop frames its mission as making ramen — broth, noodles and chashu — that cannot be replicated elsewhere.
chef_bio.specialty: A 'Minoh-style' tonkotsu — distinct from Kyushu tonkotsu — built on a creamy white broth of pork skull and knuckle bones, chicken carcass and chicken feet (momiji), finished with quality back fat, pork skin and plenty of vegetables, then simmered for 24+ hours. The flagship bowl is the special tonkotsu ramen with straight thin noodles, soft sweet chashu, green onion and bean sprouts; the kitchen also offers shoyu, miso, and mayu (burnt-garlic-oil) variations.

anecdotes.text: The shop is regarded as a rarity in Kyoto for being a dedicated pork-bone (tonkotsu) specialist rather than the city's more common lighter styles.
The broth is built from pork skull and knuckle bones plus chicken carcass and chicken feet, back fat, pork skin and vegetables, simmered for 24+ hours.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site and Osumituki confirm owner-chef 岩﨑昭一 (Iwasaki Shoichi), the March 11 2013 opening in Nishinokyo (Sanjokai arcade, near Nijo Station), ~15 years' training at a tonkotsu shop in Minoh (箕面), Osaka — his hometown, which he honors by naming the style 'Minoh tonkotsu' — the 24-hour broth (pork skull/knuckle, chicken carcass, chicken feet/momiji, back fat, pork skin, vegetables), the off-odor-suppressed 'umami/richness/depth' aim, and its rarity as a Kyoto tonkotsu specialist.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood ramen counter with a mobile-phone ordering system and self-serve sides; Japanese-language menu and a little Japanese will make ordering smoother, though pointing works fine.

kyr_ichiren_kyoto.gf_detail: No gluten-free provision. This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop: the signature bowls use thin/thick wheat noodles in pork-and-chicken or fish-dashi broths, and standard ramen tare contains wheat-based soy sauce. No dedicated gluten-free menu, no allergen statement, and no celiac-safe handling is published. Not safe for celiacs; even the soy milk yuzu bowl is served over wheat noodles.
kyr_ichiren_kyoto.vegan_detail: Not a vegan shop. The two core bowls are pork-bone/chicken broth (一蓮) and fish-dashi broth (紗), each topped with tsukune (meatball) and chashu/egg. The 豆乳柚子 (soy milk yuzu) bowl is creamy but is finished with roasted bacon, so it is not vegan, and no vegan-modified version is advertised. A diner could ask, but no plant-based ramen is offered.
kyr_ichiren_kyoto.hours_raw: 11:00-21:00 (changes by season / details announced on Instagram). Tabelog lists 11:30-18:00. Hours change seasonally.
kyr_ichiren_kyoto.notes: [Mom & Pop] ichiren is a newer yuzu-ramen specialist tucked into an alley just off Ninenzaka, a couple of minutes' walk below Kiyomizu-dera and Kodai-ji, opened in May 2021. It is a fresh brand launched by the family behind Motomachi Ramen (元町ラーメン), a Kyoto ramen name carried across three ge

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto — a new concept from the three-generation Motomachi Ramen family, set in a renovated traditional wooden machiya on Ninenzaka.
chef_bio.background: ichiren is a newer yuzu-ramen specialist tucked into an alley just off Ninenzaka, a couple of minutes' walk below Kiyomizu-dera and Kodai-ji, opened May 16, 2021. It is a fresh brand launched by the family behind Motomachi Ramen (元町ラーメン), a Kyoto ramen name carried across three generations, so the bowls draw on a long local lineage while being reworked into something refined and contemporary.
chef_bio.philosophy: To carry forward Kyoto tradition while evolving it into a refined, distinctly Kyoto ramen — built around yuzu and a calm white-and-yuzu-toned interior meant to be welcoming for solo diners and especially women.
chef_bio.specialty: Yuzu-forward Kyoto ramen. The namesake 一蓮 (Ichiren) is a rich double broth of pork bone and chicken bones brightened with yuzu; 紗 (Sara) is a clearer fish-dashi bowl (grilled flying fish, bonito, mackerel, sardine) also scented with yuzu; and the 豆乳柚子 (soy milk yuzu) bowl is creamy yet light. Bowls come with tsukune, and tables offer tororo kombu, yuzu-shichimi and yuzu-kosho to shift the flavor mid-meal.

anecdotes.text: A new brand from the three-generation Kyoto ramen house Motomachi Ramen (元町ラーメン), aiming to inherit tradition while offering a more refined bowl.
Designed by a female owner around a soft, inviting white-and-yuzu-colored space so that solo diners and women feel comfortable.
Lanterns in the shop were made by Kojima Shoten, a well-known Kyoto lantern atelier, reinforcing the machiya atmosphere.
The signature yuzu ramen is presented as a refined Kyoto experience, and tables provide tororo kombu, yuzu-shichimi and yuzu-kosho to vary the taste.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ichiren's official site and Kyorism confirm the May 16 2021 opening on Ninenzaka (near Kiyomizu-dera/Kodai-ji) in a renovated machiya, the three-generation Motomachi Ramen (元町ラーメン) lineage, the female owner and women-welcoming white-and-yuzu interior, the yuzu-forward 一蓮 (pork+chicken) / 紗 (fish dashi: flying fish, bonito, mackerel, sardine) / 豆乳柚子 bowls at ~¥1,000 with tsukune, the Kojima Shoten (小島商店) lanterns, and the tororo-kombu/yuzu-shichimi/yuzu-kosho condiments.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core bowls are wheat-noodle ramen in pork/chicken and fish-dashi broths; no gluten-free noodles or gluten-free menu are offered, so the kitchen is wheat-heavy and not celiac-appropriate.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Even the plant-leaning soy milk yuzu bowl is finished with roasted bacon, and broths are animal-based; no vegan preparation is described.

cultural_comfort.note: A polished, tourist-area yuzu-ramen shop near Kiyomizu-dera designed to welcome solo diners and women; staff are used to visitors, though a few words of Japanese and a friendly konnichiwa help.

kyr_akichan_ramen.gf_detail: Not gluten-free / not celiac-safe. The dish is wheat ramen noodles (flat noodles from Shinjuku Daruma Seimensho) in a soy-seasoned broth (wheat-based shoyu tare typical of the style). No gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen accommodations are mentioned anywhere.
kyr_akichan_ramen.vegan_detail: No vegan or vegetarian options. The signature chuka soba is built on a pork-based clear broth (清湯) with sharp soy/salt seasoning and is topped with chashu pork belly, so the broth and standard bowls contain animal products.
kyr_akichan_ramen.hours_raw: Sun-Thu 11:00-19:00; Fri, Sat and holidays 11:00-21:00. Open year-round including New Year.
kyr_akichan_ramen.notes: [Mom & Pop] Akichan Ramen opened on September 4, 2025, a short walk from Ono Station near Zuishin-in temple, becoming what local press called the first 'chan-kei' (ちゃん系) ramen shop to land in Kyoto. It belongs to the Chan-noren guild (ちゃんのれん組合), a federation of Tokyo shops such as Kanda Chie

roles: independent ramen shop / chan-noren guild member
chef_bio.background: Akichan Ramen opened on September 4, 2025, a short walk from Ono Station near Zuishin-in temple, becoming what local press called the first 'chan-kei' (ちゃん系) ramen shop to land in Kyoto. It belongs to the Chan-noren guild (ちゃんのれん組合), a federation of Tokyo shops such as Kanda Chie-chan, Shinjuku Ecchan, and Ikebukuro Hiro-chan that brought this style westward.
chef_bio.philosophy: Faithfully recreate the Kanto 'chan-kei' bowl — layered umami, rendered pork fat richness, and a clean clear broth — for Kyoto diners, with noodles kept slightly separate from the broth for texture.
chef_bio.specialty: Chuka soba (中華そば) — a Tokyo-style clear, fat-rich pork broth with sharp soy-and-salt seasoning, served with generous chashu pork belly, deeply flavored bamboo shoots, and white negi over flat, smooth specialty noodles from Shinjuku Daruma Seimensho. A favorite move is adding a raw egg to mellow the saltiness, often paired with negi rice.

anecdotes.text: Billed by local food media as Kyoto's first taste of the 'chan-kei' ramen wave that had been spreading through the Kanto region.
Uses flat, smooth specialty noodles sourced from Shinjuku Daruma Seimensho, a hallmark of the chan-kei guild shops.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi confirms the Sept 4 2025 opening near Ono Station/Zuishin-in (Yamashina), the billing as Kyoto's first 'chan-kei' shop, membership in the Chan-noren guild (ちゃんのれん組合: Kanda Chie-chan, Shinjuku Ecchan, Ikebukuro Hiro-chan), the clear fat-rich pork chuka-soba with chashu pork belly, seasoned bamboo shoots and white negi, flat smooth noodles from Shinjuku Daruma Seimensho, and the raw-egg add-in.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The chuka soba is seasoned with a sharp soy-and-salt tare typical of the style; soy sauce in Japanese ramen is normally wheat-based, so the broth should be assumed to contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is a pork-based clear consomme and bowls are topped with chashu pork belly, so all standard items contain animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A small local ramen counter with ticket-machine ordering and no reservations or English menu noted, so a little Japanese or pointing helps, though the system is straightforward.

kyr_yume_wa_chikara_nari.gf_detail: Not safe for celiac/gluten-free diners. This is a Jiro-style ramen shop built around house-made ultra-thick wheat noodles and a soy (shoyu) tare, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat. The broth is pork-based and bowls are loaded with wheat noodles, so gluten is unavoidable. No gluten-free menu, noodle substitute, or allergen accommodation is advertised. Abura soba (brothless) is also wheat noodles. Treat as off-limits if you require strict GF.
kyr_yume_wa_chikara_nari.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. Every bowl is built on a pork-bone/pork broth with large pork chunks (chashu), and standard toppings include a boiled egg. There is no vegetable or plant-based broth option advertised. The free "call" add-ons (extra vegetables, oil, garlic) sit on top of an animal-based bowl and do not make it vegan.
kyr_yume_wa_chikara_nari.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, holidays: 10:00-14:00, 17:00-21:00; Wed, Sat, Sun: 10:00-14:00 (lunch only). Opened 2024-07-23. Hours can shift per the shop's social media.
kyr_yume_wa_chikara_nari.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner is a well-known local Jiro-style ramen proprietor who has long been tied to this Fushimi corner. He previously ran 'Ramen Dai' and later 'Gatts K Ramen' at this same location, and also did a stint training at 'Yume o Katare,' the famous Jiro-style shop. After stepping a

chef_bio.origin: Fushimi-ku, Kyoto — a ramen battleground near Ryukoku University
chef_bio.background: The owner is a well-known local Jiro-style ramen proprietor long tied to this Fushimi corner on Shidan-dori. Over the years he has run several shops in the area — 'Ramen Dai,' 'Gatts K Ramen,' and 'Ryu no Sakura' — and completed a short training stint at 'Yume o Katare,' the celebrated Jiro-style shop. After stepping away, he returned to the neighborhood, on the spot that once housed 'Ramen Dai,' to open this shop in summer 2024.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop name '夢は力なり' means 'a dream is strength' — an aspirational banner from an owner who left and came back to feed his old neighborhood, carrying the lineage of the Jiro-style shops he trained in and ran before.
chef_bio.specialty: A non-emulsified Jiro bowl: a clean, sharply soy-forward, non-emulsified shoyu broth (rather than the thick cloudy emulsified style), paired with house-made wavy ultra-thick chewy noodles, big chunks of pork, a boiled egg, and a hit of black pepper. Diners customize with the free 'call' system — extra vegetables, oil (abura), and garlic — over generous portions (roughly 300g standard). Aburasoba-style eating is part of the appeal.

anecdotes.text: Local food press framed the 2024 opening as a 'famous proprietor returning' to the ramen-dense Fushimi area, on the corner that once held his earlier shop Ramen Dai.
The broth is described as soy-sharp and clearly defined — a non-emulsified style, distinguishing it from the heavier emulsified Jiro bowls — over self-made thick, wavy, springy noodles.
The owner completed a short training stint at 'Yume o Katare,' a celebrated Jiro-style shop, before returning to run this Fushimi counter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kyotopi (kyotopi.jp/articles/l1ige) reports the summer-2024 opening by a well-known local proprietor formerly of Ramen Dai, Gatts K Ramen and Ryu no Sakura, who trained briefly at Yume o Katare; it describes a non-emulsified shoyu Jiro broth, house-made thick wavy noodles, ticket-machine ordering, counter seating and a free topping 'call' system.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is a soy (shoyu) tare-based Jiro ramen; Japanese soy sauce / shoyu tare is brewed with wheat in nearly all cases, so the broth seasoning itself contains gluten in addition to the wheat noodles.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are built on pork/pork-bone broth with pork chashu and egg; no plant-based broth or vegan option is offered, so there is no vegan-safe preparation to protect from cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills, cash-only Jiro-style counter shop where ordering runs on the Jiro "call" system (vegetables/oil/garlic) in Japanese — comfortable if you know the basic ramen ritual, but no English support is advertised.

kyr_maruta_shoten.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation found. The ramen is built on wheat noodles with a wheat-based soy sauce (shoyu) tare over a pork clear broth, so the signature bowls are not celiac-safe. Evening yakitori items often carry wheat-based tare/seasoning as well. No allergen handling or dedicated equipment is documented.
kyr_maruta_shoten.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly venue. The core ramen uses a pork-bone clear broth (豚骨清湯) with pork chashu, and the evening menu centers on chicken yakitori, tsukune, and grilled pork. No vegan or vegetarian ramen or dishes were found.
kyr_maruta_shoten.hours_raw: 11:00-14:45, 17:30-22:30 (lunch ramen / evening izakaya); Sunday closed. Some sources list lunch ending around 14:00.
kyr_maruta_shoten.notes: [Mom & Pop] The owner trained at a ramen shop before opening Maruta Shoten in late May 2025, then built it as a two-faced (二毛作) neighborhood spot near Maruta-cho Shichihonmatsu in Kyoto's Nakagyo ward.

chef_bio.background: The owner trained at a ramen shop before opening Maruta Shoten on May 30, 2025, then built it as a two-faced (二毛作) neighborhood spot near Maruta-cho Shichihonmatsu in Kyoto's Nakagyo ward.
chef_bio.philosophy: By day a straightforward ramen counter, by evening a yakitori-focused izakaya — one small kitchen serving comforting, restrained Kyoto flavors from midday to night.
chef_bio.specialty: A nostalgic Kyoto-style pork clear-broth (豚清湯) shoyu chuka-soba, restrained and lightly seasoned in the classic Kyoto manner — reviewers liken it to the city's pork-bone shops of 30 years ago — and piled generously with chashu, sometimes arranged petal-style (花びらチャーシュー). The owner's ramen-shop training also shows up at night in the grilled pork.

anecdotes.text: The shop runs as a 二毛作 (two-crop) operation: lunch (11:00–14:00) is a dedicated light pork clear-broth ramen service, while evenings turn into a charcoal yakitori izakaya.
Reviewers describe a nostalgic, lightly-seasoned Kyoto pork clear-broth shoyu bowl with thick straight noodles and an abundant chashu portion, including a petal-arranged (花びらチャーシュー) version.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: gcjapan-kyoto.com and osumituki.com both date the opening to May 30, 2025 in Nakagyo-ku near Maruta-cho Shichihonmatsu, describe the 二毛作 lunch-ramen / evening-yakitori model, a nostalgic Kyoto pork clear-broth (清湯) shoyu chuka-soba with thick straight noodles and generous (petal-style) chashu, and roughly 30 seats.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The bowl is described as a 醤油 (soy sauce) shoyu tare over Kyoto pork clear broth; standard Japanese shoyu is wheat-based, so the tare should be assumed to contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is pork-bone clear soup and toppings include pork chashu; evening dishes center on chicken and pork, indicating heavy animal-product use throughout the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood spot with no indication of English service; basic Japanese or a translation app will help, especially as it shifts to an izakaya in the evening.

kyr_menya_roman.gf_detail: Standard wheat ramen: medium-thin straight wheat noodles from the long-established Kyoto noodle maker 麺屋棣鄂 (est. 1931), plus a soy-based (shoyu) tare and table-side soy sauce — all wheat-containing. No gluten-free noodles or menu noted; not safe for celiac diners.
kyr_menya_roman.vegan_detail: The house soup is a chicken-bone-and-vegetable paitan (鶏ガラ・野菜) using Satsuma Chiran chicken, and signature bowls include chicken char siu, Kyoto nine-scallion chicken ramen and wagyu items — all animal-based. No vegetarian or vegan ramen is advertised.
kyr_menya_roman.notes: [Mom & Pop] 麺家ろまん opened on January 29, 2026, in the space that previously housed the standing izakaya "すたんど ろまん家" near Kyoto Station, just west of Kyoto Tower. It is a ramen conversion of that yakitori-izakaya operation (the Kyoto "浪漫家／ろまん家" group), reborn as a chicken-paitan specialist.

roles: Former standing izakaya converted to ramen by the Kyoto 浪漫家／ろまん家 group
chef_bio.origin: 下京区東塩小路町 — a few minutes west of Kyoto Station / Kyoto Tower.
chef_bio.background: 麺家ろまん opened on January 29, 2026, in the space that previously housed the standing izakaya "すたんど ろまん家" near Kyoto Station, just west of Kyoto Tower. It is a ramen conversion of that yakitori-izakaya operation (the Kyoto "浪漫家／ろまん家" group), reborn as a chicken-paitan specialist.
chef_bio.philosophy: An approachable, Kyoto-leaning take on chicken paitan built around quality branded chicken and a respected local noodle maker, served as easy, sit-and-slurp comfort food a short walk from the station.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is the 鶏白湯ラーメン (chicken paitan, 1,000 yen): a chicken-bone-and-vegetable potage-style broth made with Satsuma Chiran chicken (さつま知覧どり), finished with a soy-based tare and paired with medium-thin straight wheat noodles from the historic Kyoto noodle house 麺屋棣鄂 (founded 1931). The broth leans gentle and creamy, opening up as you stir the bowl and add pepper or the table soy sauce.

anecdotes.text: The shop is a direct conversion of the group's standing izakaya すたんど ろまん家, which is why it keeps the "ろまん" name from the parent yakitori-izakaya brand.
The chicken paitan uses Satsuma Chiran chicken (さつま知覧どり) for the broth, and the noodles come from the long-running Kyoto noodle maker 麺屋棣鄂, established in 1931.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com (224634) confirms the Jan 29, 2026 opening in Shimogyo-ku (東塩小路町) near Kyoto Station as a conversion of the すたんど ろまん家 standing izakaya, a ¥1,000 鶏白湯 built on chicken bones and vegetables with さつま知覧どり and a soy tare, and medium-thin straight noodles from 麺屋棣鄂 (est. 1931).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is finished with a soy-based (shoyu) seasoning and soy sauce is available at the table for adjustment — standard wheat-containing shoyu, not gluten-free.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, walk-in ramen counter by Kyoto Station with QR-code/mobile ordering, so a non-Japanese-speaking diner can manage, but there is no confirmed English support or allergy handling, so come prepared to point and self-cater.

kyr_kamomachi_ramen.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The noodles are wheat-based egg noodles (たまご麺) and the broth is a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which is virtually always made with wheat. Combined with the pork/chicken broth, every bowl contains gluten, and there is no gluten-free option. People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid this shop.
kyr_kamomachi_ramen.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly shop. The broth is simmered from pork bones and chicken carcasses, the noodles are egg noodles, and the tare is soy-sauce based, so the bowls are fundamentally animal-based. There is no advertised vegan or vegetable-broth ramen.
kyr_kamomachi_ramen.hours_raw: Mon-Sat and days before holidays 11:00-15:00 (L.O. 14:50) / ~17:00-22:00 (some sources say 22:30); holidays 11:00-15:00 / 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 21:00). Closed Sun (Mon closures vary by month, posted monthly on the official site).
kyr_kamomachi_ramen.notes: [Mom & Pop] 鴨町らーめん is a tiny counter-only ramen shop tucked into the Demachi neighborhood a minute's walk from Demachiyanagi Station, on a stretch with surprisingly few eateries that makes it a reliable local stop. It has been a fixture of this student-heavy corner of Sakyo Ward, beloved mor

chef_bio.background: 鴨町らーめん is a tiny counter-only ramen shop (about nine seats) tucked into the Demachi neighborhood a minute's walk east of Demachiyanagi Station, on a stretch with surprisingly few eateries that makes it a reliable local stop. It has been a fixture of this student-heavy corner of Sakyo Ward, beloved more by neighbors and Kyoto University-area regulars than by tourists.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop sums itself up as 「味よし 麺よし 心よし」 — good taste, good noodles, good heart — and the spirit shows in small touches like complimentary house-made kimchi offered on request and uncooked take-home noodles to enjoy at home.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature bowl is a mild tonkotsu-shoyu ramen: pork bones and chicken carcasses, carefully cleaned, are simmered for hours with several kinds of aromatic vegetables into a broth that is slightly thick and mellow on the palate, with the pork richness leading over the soy. It is paired with straight medium-thin noodles and fatty, naturally sweet braised chashu. The menu is broad for such a small shop — miso (a blend of several misos), Hakata-style, tantanmen and hearty set meals among them.

anecdotes.text: Regulars and writers single out the hospitality as much as the bowl: the owner and staff are described as approachable and as giving 「丁寧で気持ちがよい接客」 (courteous, pleasant service) — fitting the shop's mellow tonkotsu-shoyu reputation.
Ask and they'll set out free house-made kimchi alongside table condiments like spicy miso and pepper; they also sell uncooked ramen to take home and prepare yourself.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kyoto-gourmet.info and kyotopi (SiMPC) describe a counter-only Demachiyanagi shop with pork-bone-over-soy broth, medium-thin straight noodles, fatty-sweet chashu, free house-made kimchi and take-home noodles; the official site (kamomachi.com) carries the motto 味よし麺よし心よし and confirms a pork-bone/chicken-carcass broth simmered for hours with aromatic vegetables, ~9 counter seats and a miso-blend option.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone soy-sauce) base; soy-sauce tare of this kind is virtually always made with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is simmered from pork bones and chicken carcasses, so all ramen here is animal-based and unsuitable for vegans/vegetarians.

positives.text: Noodles are explicitly egg noodles (たまご麺) — relevant for both egg and wheat allergies.

cultural_comfort.note: A small local counter shop in a student neighborhood with warm, attentive hosts; little to no English is expected, so a few words of Japanese or pointing at the menu will go a long way.

kyr_kirameki_japan.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop built around house-made noodles, with a chicken-paitan broth and shoyu/shio tare. House-made wheat noodles plus a typically wheat-containing soy tare make every signature bowl unsafe for celiac diners, and no gluten-free option is offered.
kyr_kirameki_japan.vegan_detail: The kitchen is centered on chicken paitan (chicken white broth) and chashu pork, with egg toppings; there is no vegan or vegetarian ramen on the menu and no plant-based broth alternative.
kyr_kirameki_japan.notes: キラメキ☆JAPAN is one of the founding Kyoto shops of the Kirameki brand operated by Kirameki no Mirai Co., Ltd., a group that has grown to more than thirty ramen shops across Kyoto, Osaka, Shiga, Nara and even Shanghai. This counter-only Demachiyanagi spot opened in January 2016 and

roles: Kirameki no Mirai Co., Ltd. (operating company / brand)
chef_bio.origin: Kyoto, part of the Kirameki group founded and headquartered in the Kansai region (headquarters and noodle factory relocated in August 2023).
chef_bio.background: キラメキ☆JAPAN is one of the Kirameki brand's Kyoto shops, operated by Kirameki no Mirai Co., Ltd., a Kansai group that has grown to more than twenty ramen shops across Kyoto, Osaka, Shiga and Nara — plus locations in Shanghai — and openly aims at a '30-shop' target. This counter-only Demachiyanagi-area spot (Tanaka-Monzencho, Sakyo Ward) opened on January 15, 2016 with about twelve seats, built around the company's signature chicken-paitan style.
chef_bio.philosophy: The group's stated belief is that the star of ramen is the noodle itself — 'ラーメンの主役は麺' — which is why every shop continues to make its noodles in-house rather than buying them in.
chef_bio.specialty: Tori-paitan ramen — a creamy, rich-yet-not-heavy chicken white broth paired with house-made noodles, alongside crowd favorites like the 醤油のキラメキ (shoyu) bowl and the hearty キラメキ二朗 (Jiro-style) bowl.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen finishes its chicken-paitan bowls with bright touches such as a slice of lemon and chopped raw onion, so the soup reads creamy and full from black pepper yet stays refreshingly light rather than heavy.
Fans describe the tori-paitan as having an almost carbonara-like richness from the creamy broth clinging to the house-made noodles.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog (26026867) dates the opening to Jan 15, 2016, a ~12-seat counter-only shop in Tanaka-Monzencho (Sakyo-ku) with tori-paitan and 醤油のキラメキ / キラメキ二朗 bowls finished with lemon and raw onion. The Kirameki no Mirai company site states the '主役は麺' philosophy, an Aug-2023 HQ/factory move, a shop list spanning Kyoto, Osaka, Shiga, Nara and Shanghai (about two dozen locations) and a '30-shop' goal.

gf_cross_contamination.text: House-made wheat noodles are the centerpiece of the shop, so flour and wheat are handled throughout the kitchen and shared boiling water is used for all bowls.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Signature bowls include a shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen, and Japanese ramen soy tare almost always contains wheat-based soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are chicken-based (tori-paitan) and bowls are topped with pork chashu and egg, so all shared soup, surfaces and utensils carry animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, busy 12-seat counter ramen bar where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will carry you through; no special foreigner-facing service should be expected.

kyr_kouiumonya_ro_ji.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The tantanmen uses wheat noodles (thin noodles from Kushiro Seimen) and a sesame-based tantan tare that, like virtually all Japanese ramen, relies on wheat-containing soy sauce. No gluten-free noodle or dedicated prep is mentioned on any source. Celiac diners should not eat the ramen here.
kyr_kouiumonya_ro_ji.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature tantanmen is built on a meat broth with large chunks of ground pork, and sides are pork karaage and chicken wings. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered or advertised.
kyr_kouiumonya_ro_ji.hours_raw: Tabelog: 11:00-22:30 (Mon-Sun and holidays). Official / Leaf KYOTO: 11:00-14:00, 17:00-24:00 (L.O. 23:45). Irregular days off.
kyr_kouiumonya_ro_ji.notes: [Mom & Pop] こういうもん家 Ro-ji opened on August 5, 2019, tucked down a narrow alley (the "ro-ji" of its name) just a minute south of Demachiyanagi Station. The space was originally a private company warehouse, reborn as a half-open, yatai (food-stall) style counter with no partitions — the kind o

chef_bio.background: こういうもん家 Ro-ji opened on August 5, 2019, tucked down a narrow alley (the "ro-ji" of its name) just south of Demachiyanagi Station. The space was originally a company warehouse, reborn as a half-open, yatai (food-stall) style counter — the kind of hidden-alley spot you stumble onto and feel you've found a secret.
chef_bio.philosophy: A creamy tantanmen tuned to please across age groups rather than to chase extreme spice — approachable comfort food served stall-style, equally happy as a quick lunch or a late-night drinking spot.
chef_bio.specialty: Creamy, mild tantanmen. The house bowl leans on a rich sesame aroma with gentle, not-overpowering heat, topped with ground pork; on request the kitchen will hold back the finishing chili oil (rayu) for milder palates. Variations include a spicy 大辛担々麺, a tomato トマ担麺, and a curry カレー担々麺, and a popular half-size (the local move is to order izakaya snacks first and close the night with a half bowl, or turn the leftover soup into 'tantan rice').

anecdotes.text: Thin noodles are sourced from Kushiro Seimen, a Fushimi-based noodle maker, and served slightly soft; the counter sets out scorched garlic and sansho pepper so you can shift the flavor as you eat.
The shop doubles as a casual izakaya in the evening, with house-made karaage (fried chicken) as a signature side and popular takeout item alongside the noodles.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com (127167) and leafkyoto.net confirm the Aug 5, 2019 opening in a converted warehouse as an alley yatai near Demachiyanagi, a mild-and-creamy sesame tantanmen with half-size and 'tantan rice,' Kushiro Seimen (Fushimi) noodles and scorched-garlic/sansho condiments; the official ro-ji.com lists the spicy/tomato/curry variations, the option to omit the finishing rayu, and karaage as a signature/takeout item.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Tantanmen uses wheat ramen noodles (Kushiro Seimen) boiled in shared water; no gluten-free handling is mentioned.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No source specifies the tare ingredients, but a sesame tantan tare of this style standardly uses wheat-based soy sauce; treat as containing wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is meat-based with ground pork topping; no vegan preparation described.

positives.text: Kitchen will omit the finishing chili oil on request, so the bowl can be made milder.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, half-open food-stall counter where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will get you by; no English service is advertised, so a few Japanese words help.

kyr_chuka_soba_mimio.gf_detail: No gluten-free options. The signature 中華そば uses wheat straight noodles and a soy-sauce-seasoned chicken-and-dashi broth (soy sauce is normally wheat-based), with pork-belly chashu. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated prep, or celiac accommodation is mentioned anywhere. Not suitable for celiacs.
kyr_chuka_soba_mimio.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The shop is built around a chicken-bone and fish/dashi broth with domestic pork-belly chashu; the soy-sauce tare is animal-adjacent and side dishes include pidan (century egg). No vegetable/vegan broth or plant-based bowl is offered or mentioned.
kyr_chuka_soba_mimio.hours_raw: Wed-Sun 12:00-14:00, 18:00-23:00 / closed Mon and Tue (hours should be confirmed)
kyr_chuka_soba_mimio.notes: [Mom & Pop] Mimio is a Kyoto institution that spent many years as a beloved late-night, after-drinks ramen haunt in the Gion entertainment district, where it quietly drew a following that included entertainers and professional chefs. In March 2016 it relocated across the city to a quieter sp

chef_bio.background: Mimio is a Kyoto institution that spent many years as a beloved late-night, after-drinks ramen haunt in the Gion entertainment district, where it quietly drew a following that included entertainers and professional chefs. In March 2016 it relocated across the city to a quieter spot in Yoshida, Sakyo Ward, near Jingu-Marutamachi, where it carries on the same bowl.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than the usual fast-turnover ramen counter, the owner deliberately designed Mimio as a place to settle in — with counter, tables and a tatami room — so guests can slowly enjoy a drink alongside the bowl. The broth is portioned so you can comfortably finish it to the last sip.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature 名物中華そば is a clear, gentle soy-sauce ramen: a broth drawn carefully from chicken bones and dashi with select ingredients, paired with thin, springy straight noodles and a standout chashu of domestic pork belly sourced from a long-established butcher, simmered until it melts on the tongue. Pidan (century egg) is a popular small plate, and the same broth is even turned into a curry.

anecdotes.text: Before its move, Mimio was a long-loved spot in Gion to cap off a night of drinking, frequented by celebrities and fellow chefs.
The noodles are straight noodles from a Kyoto noodle maker founded in 1879, and the chashu uses domestic pork belly from an established butcher, braised until tender.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: mypl.net (newopen_sakyokita, sid=47151) documents the Mar 9, 2016 relocation to Yoshida/Sakyo-ku after long years in Gion (loved by celebrities and chefs), counter/table/tatami seating for lingering over a drink, a broth built to be drunk to the last drop, straight noodles from an 1879 noodle maker, domestic pork-belly chashu from an established butcher, plus pidan and a curry.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature bowl is a soy-sauce-seasoned chicken-and-dashi ramen; soy sauce tare is normally wheat-based, so the broth should be assumed to contain wheat/gluten.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broth is built on chicken bones and fish/dashi with pork-belly chashu, and pidan (egg) is a popular side - no vegan-safe preparation is offered.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed neighborhood ramen-and-drinks spot run by a hands-on owner; little English is expected, so a few words of Japanese or pointing at the menu will go a long way.

kyr_menya_kagura.gf_detail: No gluten-free option. The bowls are built on wheat noodles (medium-thick straight noodles made with whole-grain wheat flour from a local noodle factory) and almost certainly a wheat-based shoyu tare, served in fish/chicken broth. Nothing on any page indicates gluten-free accommodation, and this is a tiny solo-run counter shop unlikely to manage cross-contamination. Not celiac-safe.
kyr_menya_kagura.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. Every bowl is animal-based: niboshi (dried sardine), bonito, kombu, clam and chicken stock, with chicken oil and chashu (pork) toppings. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.
kyr_menya_kagura.hours_raw: 11:00-14:30 / 17:30-21:30 (Tabelog lists lunch 10:30-14:30 L.O.14:15, dinner 17:30-20:00 L.O.19:45). Closed Wednesdays; occasional irregular closures.

The new shop is run by family of the

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Jodoji / Ginkaku-ji area, Sakyo Ward), Japan
chef_bio.background: Menya Kagura opened on February 3, 2021 in the Jodoji / Ginkaku-ji area of Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, taking over the address of Menya Himawari, a beloved salt-ramen shop that had operated there since 2006 before relocating to Shizuoka in November 2020. The new shop is run by the former Himawari owner's brother and opened under the former owner's supervision, carrying the lineage forward in the same little space.
chef_bio.philosophy: A fish-driven ramen specialist standing apart from Kyoto's pork-bone-heavy norm, offering deliberately different lunch (lighter, delicate shio/shoyu) and dinner (richer niboshi) styles from one small counter.
chef_bio.specialty: Niboshi (dried sardine) ramen. The kitchen builds its stock from multiple dried sardines, thick-shaved bonito, kombu, clams and chicken. The signature 濃厚煮干そば is a mild-but-rich niboshi bowl with controlled bitterness and a clean sweetness, while the lighter 淡麗醤油そば and 淡麗塩そば show off fish-forward umami with aromatic chicken oil on top. Medium-thick straight whole-grain wheat noodles from a local noodle maker (麺屋棣鄂) come with generous, well-seared chashu, nori and scallion.

anecdotes.text: The shop sits in the exact former location of Menya Himawari, a salt-ramen shop open since 2006 that moved to Shizuoka in November 2020; Menya Kagura opened there in February 2021 under the former Himawari owner's supervision.

In a Kyoto ramen scene dominated by pork-bone broths, Kagura's dedicated niboshi/seafood focus near Ginkaku-ji and Kyoto University is described as a rare specialty, with the owner running service solo.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com (145534) confirms the Feb 3, 2021 opening in the former Menya Himawari space (salt ramen since 2006, moved to Shizuoka Nov 2020), operation by the previous owner's brother under his supervision, a sardine/bonito/kombu/clam/chicken stock, 濃厚煮干 and 淡麗 (醤油/塩) bowls, chicken oil, and medium-thick whole-grain straight noodles from 麺屋棣鄂 with chashu, nori and scallion.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Bowls are built on wheat noodles and a fish/shoyu base; the shoyu tare is the standard wheat-containing type with no gluten-free alternative mentioned on any source.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All broths use animal stock (dried sardine, bonito, kombu, clam, chicken) with chicken oil and pork chashu; no vegan or vegetarian bowl exists, so shared pots make any vegan accommodation impossible.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny solo-run neighborhood counter shop near Ginkaku-ji where ordering is straightforward but staff likely speak little English; basic Japanese or pointing at the menu goes a long way.

kyr_biden.gf_detail: This is a standard ramen shop built on wheat. The bowls use medium-thin wheat noodles (from a Kyoto noodle maker), and the chicken-paitan broth is almost certainly seasoned with a wheat-based shoyu tare. No gluten-free noodles, dedicated preparation, or allergy accommodation is mentioned anywhere. Not suitable for celiacs or strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_biden.vegan_detail: The house style is a rich chicken (tori-paitan) broth, and the signature bowl is loaded with chicken chashu, chicken tsukune meatballs, and smoked poultry. The broth itself is animal-based, so even a no-toppings request would not be vegan. No vegetarian or vegan ramen is offered. (A cold tomato noodle and an oil/carbonara-style bowl appear on the menu but are not described as plant-based.)
kyr_biden.hours_raw: 11:30-15:30 (L.O. 15:00), 18:00-22:30 (L.O. 22:00). Sunday lunch only per Tabelog (11:30-15:00). Closed Sundays per shop guides; one source also notes Monday evenings closed.
kyr_biden.notes: [Mom & Pop] Biden opened on July 16, 2021, just north of the Kyoto Imperial Palace in the Demachi neighborhood near Demachiyanagi Station, an area with very few ramen shops. The owner had previously cooked at a ramen restaurant over in the Saiin district before striking out on his own. The s

chef_bio.origin: Kyoto (Demachi / north of the Imperial Palace)
chef_bio.background: Biden opened on July 16, 2021, just north of the Kyoto Imperial Palace in the Demachi neighborhood near Demachiyanagi Station, an area with very few ramen shops. The owner had previously cooked at a ramen restaurant over in the Saiin district before striking out on his own. The shop took over the premises of a former izakaya called YAOMON, which had closed after its previous owner fell ill, and Biden kept those izakaya bones — the tatami room and the counter — while reinventing it as a ramen specialist by day.
chef_bio.philosophy: A chicken-paitan style that is rich but elegant, a style the local guides note is rare in Kyoto, served in a relaxed, lived-in room.
chef_bio.specialty: Tori-paitan ramen (around 800 yen): a creamy-looking chicken broth that drinks surprisingly light and refined rather than heavy, paired with straight medium-thin wheat noodles from a long-established Kyoto noodle maker that give the 'patsun' snap locals favor. The bowl is unusually colorful and generous, topped with thin-sliced smoked chicken chashu, chicken tsukune meatballs, sauteed king oyster mushrooms, bell pepper, sweet thick-cut grilled scallions, and daikon sprouts.

anecdotes.text: The owner is a film and arcade-game enthusiast, and the walls of the shop are decorated with movie posters.

The space was a former izakaya (YAOMON) that closed when its previous owner became ill; Biden reused its layout, with tatami seating on one side and the counter and kitchen on the other, and still flips into an izakaya/omakase service in the evenings.
The signature feature is the thick-cut grilled scallion topping, described as a novel touch that turns sweet when chewed.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com (160101) confirms the Jul 16, 2021 opening near Demachiyanagi, the owner's prior work at a Saiin ramen shop, the takeover of the former YAOMON izakaya (closed after the owner's illness) keeping tatami and counter, a light-yet-refined ~¥800 tori-paitan with straight medium-thin Kyoto-maker noodles and a colorful topping array, plus the owner's film/arcade posters; kyoto-gourmet.info highlights the thick-cut grilled scallion.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood shop with no indication of English-language service; basic Japanese or a translation app will smooth the visit.

kyr_fukusenro_kitashirakawa_.gf_detail: Not safe for celiacs. The signature bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles, and the broth is a pork-bone/chicken (tonkotsu-shoyu) base seasoned with soy sauce, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat. There is no indication of gluten-free noodles, tamari, or any allergen protocol, and noodles are boiled in shared water. Treat as off-limits if you require strict GF.
kyr_fukusenro_kitashirakawa_.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The kitchen is built around a pork-bone and chicken broth with back fat, braised tendon, and minced Kyotamba pork; even the simplest bowls carry animal stock and pork toppings. No vegetable or vegan broth option is advertised.
kyr_fukusenro_kitashirakawa_.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-14:30 / dinner 18:00-21:30 (last order). Closed Tue and Wed (consecutive). Note: Tabelog lists closed Wed (with a Tue-Wed consecutive closure in Jan 2026), so closing-day info is inconsistent.

The team behind it studied Taiwanese street-stall noodle cooking and brought that style back to this quiet student quarter near K

roles: Taiwanese street-stall sibling of 東龍 北白川本店
chef_bio.background: 福仙楼 is the 台湾屋台 (Taiwanese street-stall) sibling of the well-known Kitashirakawa ramen shop 東龍, opened on April 30, 2009 along the same stretch of 北白川 and sharing the 第2青山荘 building (both under the parent 有限会社 潜龍). The team studied Taiwanese street-stall noodle cooking and brought that style to this quiet student quarter near Kyoto University of the Arts, running it as a counterpart to 東龍. The two brands have grown deeply intertwined over the years — the 福仙楼そば and 屋台そば bowls have at times been folded into 東龍's own lineup, so its identity as a fully separate shop has blurred; check current status before a visit.
chef_bio.philosophy: Generous, hearty Taiwanese-street-stall-style bowls at student-friendly prices — comfort ramen made to fill you up rather than to chase trends.
chef_bio.specialty: 福仙楼そば — a rich pork-bone-and-chicken broth finished with back fat and a soy (shoyu) tare, poured over medium-thick, flat, straight house-made noodles and crowned with slow-braised tendon and juicy minced Kyotamba heritage pork, plus bean sprouts, scallion and garlic. The menu runs from the base 屋台そば up through larger 福スペシャル and チャーシュー麺 versions that pile on more pork.

anecdotes.text: The shop's identity is rooted in Taiwanese 屋台 (street-stall) cooking: its base bowl is literally called 屋台そば, and the house style was developed by studying Taiwanese street-noodle technique before adapting it to Kyoto.
福仙楼 and 東龍 are sister operations sharing the same 北白川 building, so the creamy 東龍そば and the soy-rich 福仙楼そば trace to steps from each other.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com (191010) dates 福仙楼's opening to Apr 30, 2009 as the Taiwanese-street-stall sibling of 東龍 sharing the 第2青山荘 building, describes a pork-bone/chicken broth with back fat, shoyu tare, braised tendon and minced Kyotamba pork, and states it closed May 10, 2020 with its menu absorbed into 東龍; the official tonryu.net still lists 福仙楼 with its 屋台そば / 福仙楼そば bowls, hence the hedge on current status.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat ramen noodles are the base of every bowl and are boiled in shared water; there is no gluten-free noodle or separate-pot option mentioned.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth is a pork-bone/chicken base finished with a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; Japanese soy sauce is typically brewed with wheat, so the soup itself is not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All bowls are built on animal stock (pork bone, chicken, back fat) with pork and tendon toppings; no vegan or vegetable broth is offered, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: A small neighborhood ramen counter run by a local Kyoto operator; menus and signage are in Japanese, so a little Japanese or a translation app will smooth the visit.

kyr_ramen_arashiyama_chikuri.gf_detail: No gluten-free option. All bowls are built on wheat ramen noodles (sourced from Kiyokawa Seimen, including "whole-grain" noodles used for the vegan bowls — whole grain still means wheat, not gluten-free), and the tare is naturally-fermented shiro-tamari or soy sauce, both of which are wheat-based. There is no indication of a gluten-free noodle or a wheat-free seasoning, and no dedicated handling for celiac diners. Not suitable for strict gluten avoidance.
kyr_ramen_arashiyama_chikuri.vegan_detail: Genuine vegan bowls are a fixed part of the menu, not an afterthought: a Kyoto-vegetable salt ramen, a "tonkotsu-style" vegetable ramen (plant-based, mimicking pork-bone richness), and a 100% vegan Shinshu-miso ramen, all on whole-grain (wheat) noodles, around 2,000 yen. However this is a small counter shop whose core trade is chicken-clear, chicken-paitan and spiny-lobster-paitan broths with pork chashu, so the vegan bowls are prepared in the same kitchen alongside animal broths. Good for plant-based diners by ingredient, but ask about shared equipment if you need strict separation.
kyr_ramen_arashiyama_chikuri.hours_raw: 11:00-19:00 (hours and closing days may be irregular)
kyr_ramen_arashiyama_chikuri.notes: [Mom & Pop] RAMEN Arashiyama Chikurintei opened in December 2023, just off the famous bamboo grove in Saga-Arashiyama, run by a trained Japanese-cuisine (washoku) chef and his wife. The couple bring a kaiseki-style attention to stock-making and ingredient sourcing to a bowl of ramen.

chef_bio.background: RAMEN Arashiyama Chikurintei opened in December 2023, just off the famous bamboo grove in Saga-Arashiyama, run by a trained Japanese-cuisine (washoku) chef and his wife. The couple bring a kaiseki-style attention to stock-making and ingredient sourcing to a bowl of ramen.
chef_bio.philosophy: Quality ingredients and meticulous, additive-free preparation: named-breed chicken bones, kombu and bonito for the stocks, additive-free Kyoto pork for the chashu, and specially-milled noodles from Kiyokawa Seimen. The kitchen also keeps a real plant-based line so vegan and international visitors are not left out.
chef_bio.specialty: Their signature is the ise-ebi (spiny lobster) paitan ramen, a creamy broth built from Nagoya Cochin and Daiyama chicken bones and Ibaraki pork and finished with extract pressed from spiny-lobster heads, served with additive-free Kyoto-pork rare chashu and a shrimp terrine; the clear chicken (tori chintan) bowl, seasoned with Guerande salt or naturally-fermented shiro-tamari, shows the same restraint.

anecdotes.text: The spiny-lobster paitan gets its depth from broth pressed out of the lobster heads, layered over a chicken-and-pork base.
Run by a washoku professional and his wife, the shop is described locally as standing out as the best ramen in the Arashiyama area.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: osumituki.com (201250) dates the opening to Dec 18, 2023 near the Saga-Arashiyama bamboo grove, run by a washoku chef and his wife; it details the ise-ebi paitan (Nagoya Cochin + Daiyama chicken bones, Ibaraki pork, lobster-head extract, additive-free Kyoto-pork rare chashu, shrimp terrine), a tori-chintan seasoned with Guerande salt or shiro-tamari, Kiyokawa Seimen noodles, a vegan line, and calls it the area's best ramen.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All ramen, including the vegan bowls, uses wheat noodles; the seasoning is wheat-based shiro-tamari or soy sauce. No gluten-free noodle or tare exists here, so the kitchen has no gluten-free workflow.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tare is naturally-fermented shiro-tamari (a white tamari/soy) or soy sauce, both wheat-containing.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The vegan ramen (vegetable salt, vegetable 'tonkotsu-style', and 100% vegan Shinshu-miso) is genuinely plant-based by recipe, but it is cooked in the same small kitchen as chicken-clear, chicken-paitan and spiny-lobster broths with pork chashu, so shared pots/utensils are likely.

positives.text: Multiple dedicated vegan bowls are a permanent menu item, and the kitchen emphasizes additive-free ingredients, which is reassuring for plant-based diners by ingredient.

'The kitchen emphasizes additive-free ingredients' is lifted from the NAME of the additive-free Kyoto-PORK rare-chashu ramen — a claim transplanted from the one dish a vegan cannot eat. 'Permanent men

cultural_comfort.note: A small owner-run counter shop in a heavily-touristed area with a smartphone ordering system and English-friendly vegan options, so a few words of Japanese and a polite manner go a long way, but you will likely manage.

kyr_seabura_no_kami_slurp.gf_detail: Not celiac-safe. The signature tsukemen uses straight wheat noodles (which include wheat bran) from a noodle maker, and the tare is a blend of two soy sauce varieties (wheat-based) cut with kombu water. Broth is pork-bone and chicken collagen. No gluten-free noodle or dedicated-prep option is indicated; a celiac should not eat here.
kyr_seabura_no_kami_slurp.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. Every signature bowl is built on animal stock — pork-bone/chicken-collagen broth, Iberico pork belly and low-temperature pork chashu, and soy-sauce tare. There is no plant-based ramen on the menu.
kyr_seabura_no_kami_slurp.notes: [Mom & Pop] slurp is the fourth shop from the Kansai ramen group behind セアブラノ神 (Seabura no Kami), a name that built its reputation popularizing niboshi-and-tonkotsu style ramen in Kyoto through its Mibu flagship and the Fushimi-Gōriki and Nishiki branches. Opened in 2020 near Sanjō-Karasuma,

chef_bio.background: slurp is the fourth shop from the Kansai ramen group behind セアブラノ神 (Seabura no Kami), a name that built its reputation on niboshi-and-tonkotsu style ramen topped with pork back fat. Opened in 2020 near Sanjō-Karasuma, slurp was the group's first venture into tsukemen, deliberately styled less like a traditional ramen shop and more like an upscale dining bar in black tones so that even a solo diner — including women dining alone — feels at ease walking in.
chef_bio.philosophy: Treat a single bowl of tsukemen as an entertaining, multi-course experience, and make the room approachable enough that anyone — including women dining alone — feels welcome.
chef_bio.specialty: The Iberico pork tsukemen — pitched as 'one bowl, five ways to enjoy it.' Straight noodles (from 麺屋棣鄂) are first soaked in kombu (kelp) water and eaten plain to taste their fragrance and umami, then dipped into a clear-yet-rich broth of pork bone and chicken collagen finished with premium Spanish Iberico pork; a squeeze of citrus refreshes the midpoint, and the leftover broth is cut with bonito dashi and finished over rice like a soup or risotto.

anecdotes.text: slurp was the established Seabura no Kami group's first move into tsukemen, designed as a stylish dining-bar-like space rather than a conventional ramen counter so solo and first-time diners feel comfortable.

The signature Iberico pork tsukemen is built to be eaten in stages — plain kombu-water noodles, then dipped, then brightened with citrus, then the broth finished with bonito dashi over rice — described as 'five ways to enjoy one bowl.'

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog Magazine (article 420882) identifies slurp as the Seabura no Kami group's fourth shop and first tsukemen, opened 2020 near Sanjo-Karasuma with a black-toned dining-bar design welcoming to solo diners and women; it details the Iberico pork tsukemen served 'five ways,' with kombu-water noodles from 麺屋棣鄂, a pork-bone/chicken-collagen broth, Iberico pork, a citrus refresher and a bonito-dashi rice finish.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tsukemen tare is described as a blend of two soy sauce varieties cut with kombu-infused water; standard soy sauce is wheat-based.
